docs.s: What neon1 is for, who it serves first, the values it works by, and what it leaves to others.
k: neon1 is a one-person technology practice in New York, run by me, Pradeep. The company is neon1 LLC, formed in New York on July 24, 2025, and neon1 is the name it does business under. This charter covers why neon1 exists, who it serves, and how it works. The How I work documents go into detail.
Help people and small organizations make their technology work together, improve everyday work, and keep the understanding and control to run what they own.

I work with cloud and AI software, infrastructure, and connected devices, and use them where they make the result better. For each tool or system in an engagement, the recommendation is one of seven outcomes: Outcome What it means Keep It works. Leave it alone, maybe with a note on how it's used Configure The tool you have can already do it. Turn on what's there Integrate Connect it to the other tools it should share information with Migrate Move it somewhere that fits better, with your data intact Replace Swap it for something that does the job with less effort Retire Stop paying for it and shut it down cleanly Outsource Someone else is better placed to run it, and I'll say so Moving everything to the cloud, or to an AI model, is never the default answer.

Listen first. I write down the real workflow before proposing anything. Simplicity. I pick the option with the smallest ongoing burden that still meets the need. Quality. The result works, can be recovered when it breaks, and you can run it. Transparency. Scope, price, evidence, and limits are clear before work starts. Your independence. You own your accounts and billing. You get the docs, the exports, and a clean way out. Reuse before building. Existing tools and open-source software come first. I build only the part nothing else covers.

Owner-operated service businesses and small practices losing time between email, spreadsheets, point of sale, documents, and apps that don't talk to each other. Technical small businesses that need clarity on their cloud accounts, repeatable deployments, and recovery. Individuals, homes, and connected devices , when the travel, safety, and upkeep make sense.

Some work needs a specialist or a team with round-the-clock coverage. For these, I'll refer you to someone who fits: 24/7 emergency support Safety-critical equipment Regulated professional judgment, such as legal, medical, or accounting advice Large migrations that need a team Formal security assurance, such as a penetration test or an audit opinion
Paid work is paid. Separately, I set aside a little time each month for community help, chosen at my discretion. That's a habit, not a claim to be a nonprofit.

docs.s: How everything neon1 writes is written, from policies and proposals to READMEs, commit messages, code comments, and interface text.
k: This is the main writing standard for neon1. It applies to every word neon1 publishes or ships: documents on this site, proposals, emails, READMEs, changelogs, commit messages, code comments, and the text inside an interface. Other standards add rules for particular kinds of writing and point back here.

Lead with what the reader needs. Put the answer, decision, or action first. Background comes after, and only if it helps. Use plain words. Everyday verbs, short sentences, and natural contractions. Keep an exact technical term when it carries meaning, and explain it once in terms of the reader's task. Be concrete. Name who does what, when, and what happens next. A specific detail beats a general claim. Say only what's true and supported. Keep the difference between what was planned, built, tested, released, and shown to help. Don't invent experience, numbers, quotes, or results. When something is unknown, say so. Use the fewest words that keep the full meaning. Cut framing, repetition, and filler. Don't cut a detail that explains a cause, a limit, or a consequence. Write in the right voice. "I" where Pradeep is doing the work, "neon1" for the business, and "you" for the reader. Warm through clarity and follow-through, not through reassurance.

Write like a technical business owner talking to another one: direct, candid, and specific. The care shows in what gets done for the reader, not in how the writing feels about them. Say it and stop. State what's true, what it costs, and what happens next. Don't add warmth, reassurance, or enthusiasm on top. Don't solicit. No pitch, no urgency, no "let's get started," and no telling readers how they feel or what they deserve. Argue from evidence. A number, a named method, or a real example beats an adjective. When the evidence is thin, say that. Leave the decision with the reader. Give the options and their tradeoffs. Recommend plainly when it helps, and say why. Be candid about limits. Say what neon1 doesn't do, when someone else is a better fit, and what might not work. Show values as practices. "Accounts stay in your name" says more than "we value your ownership." Talk about the work and the reader's problem, not about neon1's passion or commitment. The test: would a capable professional say this sentence across a table to a peer? If it sounds like an advertisement, a greeting card, or a pitch, rewrite it.

These are signs of writing that sounds produced rather than meant: Inflated words: leverage, utilize, robust (as praise), seamless, cutting-edge, delve, landscape, tapestry, pivotal, crucial, furthermore, moreover. Slogan sentences that sound good but say little, such as "Technology that works together, and stays yours." "Not just X, but Y," and other set-piece contrasts used for effect. A question answered right away ("Why does this matter? Because..."). Lists of exactly three used as rhythm rather than content. Dashes and semicolons in prose. Use a period or a comma instead. Absolutes such as "always," "never," and "every" unless they're literally true. Selling words in place of facts: guaranteed, best-in-class, effortless, game-changing. Soft selling: "happy to help," "I'd love to," "no pressure," "peace of mind," "worry-free," "let's get started," "reach out." Intensifiers that stand in for evidence: really, truly, genuinely, honestly, simply, just, actually, incredibly. Describing neon1's character instead of its practice: passionate, dedicated, committed to, care deeply, here for you. Telling the reader how they feel ("Worried about...?", "Tired of...?") or what they'll feel afterward. Lists, the passive voice, and formal words aren't errors on their own. Judge them by whether they help the reader.

neon1 is always lowercase, even at the start of a sentence. The company is neon1 LLC . Serial comma: "email, spreadsheets, and POS." Sentence case for titles and headings. Numbers: words for one to nine in prose, numerals for 10 and up, and numerals for measurements, money, versions, and dates in tables. Dates: "November 9, 2026" in prose, 2026-11-09 in data and file names. Times: "8am to 8pm, Eastern time." Links say where they go ("see the privacy policy "), never "click here." Code, commands, file names, and identifiers go in code formatting , copied exactly.

Different documents have different jobs. The structure follows the job. Kind Its job Structure Policy Tell people what's done with their information and their rights Short version first, then sections by question. Dated "Last updated." Plain prose, no marketing Agreement or template Record obligations exactly Defined terms, numbered sections, blanks to fill, an "example, not legal advice" note when it is one Standard Say how neon1 works and why What I do, then the reason. Present tense. No claims of certification or results Guide or how-to Help someone finish a task Who it's for, what they need, numbered steps, what to do when it goes wrong Reference Be looked up, not read through Tables and short entries, exact values, consistent order Explanation Help someone understand a topic One idea per section, in the order the reader needs them Proposal Help a client decide Their problem, the result, what's in and out, price, schedule, acceptance, next step Case study Show real work honestly Needs, Execute, Observe, Normalize, with scope and limits stated Form Capture facts Labeled blanks and checkboxes. An empty field is an open question README Help someone use or contribute to a project What it is, who it's for, status, how to run, deploy, and contribute, license Changelog Tell people what changed for them Newest first, grouped by version, written for users Commit message Explain one change to future readers Type and scope, then a plain summary. A body when the reason isn't obvious Code comment Explain intent the code can't Why, constraints, and invariants, never a narration of the next line Interface text Help someone act in the moment Short labels, verbs on buttons, errors that say what happened and how to fix it Email or message Get something done with someone The ask or answer first, context after, one clear next step The guide and reference split follows the Diátaxis framework for documentation. The documentation standard covers READMEs, changelogs, and decision records in more detail, and the code style standard covers comments and names.

Read it as the intended reader. Can they act on it? Compare it claim by claim with the sources. Nothing added, nothing overstated. Remove anything from the "avoid" list. Check names, numbers, dates, links, and code exactly. Read it aloud. Rewrite any sentence that's hard to say. Good writing that already works stays as it is. Shorter is only better when the meaning survives.

docs.s: The main development standard for neon1: the principles in priority order, what each word means, how work moves from idea to release, and where the detailed rules live.
k: This is the main development standard for neon1. It covers every project neon1 builds, for itself or for a client: websites, tools, infrastructure, automations, and AI features. It sets the principles and the order of work. The detailed rules live in the standards linked at the end, and each of them follows this one.

When two principles pull in different directions, the higher one wins. Most of the time they agree. # Principle What it means here 1 Safety Nobody is harmed, no data is lost or exposed, and nothing irreversible happens by accident. Covers security, privacy, and data integrity 2 Correctness It does what it says, including in the failure cases that matter 3 Value It solves a real need someone has today. Work that isn't needed isn't done, however interesting 4 Usability The intended person can do the task without help, on their device, including with assistive technology 5 Simplicity The fewest parts, dependencies, and concepts that meet the need. Easy to explain in a few sentences 6 Robustness It degrades visibly instead of silently, recovers from failure, and can be undone 7 Maintainability Someone else can read it, change it, and run it without the author 8 Efficiency It uses time, money, and computing in proportion to its value. Fast enough, cheap enough, measured before optimized 9 Consistency It follows the conventions of its project and of neon1, so nothing has to be relearned A few consequences of the order: A simpler design that leaves a security gap loses. A faster design that's harder to use loses unless speed is the need. Efficiency matters, but it comes after people can use and maintain the thing. Optimize what's measured, not what's guessed. Consistency is last because a convention should give way when it would make something unsafe, wrong, or unusable. When that happens, the convention gets updated rather than quietly broken.

These words come up often. Each one means something specific here. Word Meaning Mature Complete for its stated purpose, dependable in its intended workflows, documented, and recoverable. Not the same as old or large Ready Tested in conditions like real use, with known limits written down and a way back Done Built, tested, documented, reviewed, released, and handed over. Merged alone isn't done Robust Survives bad input, outages, and retries without corrupting anything, and says when it fails Simple Few parts and few concepts. Not the same as quick to write Usable The intended person finishes the task without help Valuable Someone would notice and mind if it were gone Efficient Proportionate in time, cost, and resources to what it delivers Secure Meets the agreed baseline for its data and risks, with evidence. Never a blanket claim

Every piece of work follows the same order, at whatever size fits: Reproduce. Start from something that works: an existing tool, a known pattern, or the current behavior, with a baseline measured. Integrate. Connect it into the complete path a person actually uses, end to end. Enhance. Improve what real use shows is missing or weak. Unify. Once several pieces work, share their common parts and make them consistent. Reuse comes before building. Existing tools and well-maintained open-source projects come first, checked under the technology decisions standard. Custom code covers only what nothing else does. For a bug, the order is: reproduce it, find the cause, fix it narrowly, add a test that would have caught it, and check the behavior around it.

Before v1.0.0 , a project is under initial development, and its versions say so. v1.0.0 is reserved for the first complete, dependable release of the whole intended scope, shown to work for the people it's for. Passing tests or finishing one feature doesn't make a project 1.0.0. The versioning standard defines every version number in detail.

Standard Covers Writing Every word neon1 writes, including code comments and commit messages Version control Branches, commits, merges, protection, and history Versioning and releases Version numbers, tags, changelogs, and when each number goes up Code style Names, comments, file headers, formatting, and layout Testing and review What gets tested, how changes are reviewed, and the definition of done Documentation READMEs, changelogs, decision records, and runbooks Security and data The security baseline and data handling Design and accessibility Interfaces and documents anyone can use Technology decisions Choosing tools and architecture, and counting the full cost Reliability and recovery Service targets, backups, and incidents AI quality and oversight AI features inside what neon1 builds

Code written for a client lives in a repository the client owns, under the license agreed. The handover includes how to build, test, deploy, and roll back without me. Reused open-source code keeps its license and notices, and I explain what each license allows.
I use AI tools to review code for bugs, security issues, and missing tests, alongside automated checks. I review and take responsibility for every change that ships. See How I use AI .
