docs.s: The habits behind every neon1 engagement, and what each one means in practice.
k: A good engagement leaves you better able to run your own technology, without needing me for every small change. These are the habits I follow to get there.

I ask the person who does the task to show me the last real example. I write down how often it happens, what goes wrong, and the workaround people already use. A request for "AI" sometimes turns out to need a clearer form or a shared folder, and that's a fine answer.

Accounts, billing, and recovery methods are yours, in your name. I get named, limited access that ends when the work does. The handover says who owns each account and how to leave each tool. If a tool makes it hard to export your data, I tell you before you buy it.
Charge for responsibility and useful work
Scoping, testing, documentation, and training are part of the work and part of the price. A quote covers the whole result, including that work, rather than only the time spent changing settings.
I keep five things apart: what we observed, what someone remembers, what we estimated, what a demo showed, and what we're proposing. Mixing them up leads to surprises late in a project.
A system can run around the clock while I work by appointment. Every service says who responds when something fails and when. An automatic alert isn't a staffed response, and I won't sell it as one.
Prefer the smallest solution that lasts
I check what you already pay for before adding anything new. Maintenance, vendor changes, access, and recovery all count in the decision. Free software you host yourself still costs someone's time.

I explain choices in terms of your task. Then I show the routine, you do it, and you fix one common mistake on purpose. If a tool would add work or watch your staff in ways they'd object to, that counts against it.

Before a change, I know how to undo it, how to get the data back, and how the business keeps going in the meantime. When a job needs faster response or deeper expertise than I can give, I help you find someone who can.

A project is a good fit when the problem repeats, you can describe what success looks like, the data is yours to share, the work fits the calendar, and there's a manual way to keep going if something fails. The person who pays and the person who uses the system are often different people, and I talk with both. I refer out continuous emergency support, safety-critical equipment, regulated professional judgment, specialist security assurance, and large migrations.

Projects have a written scope and a fixed price by default, with the assumptions written down. Third-party subscriptions, hardware, and travel are separate, and I prefer that vendors bill you directly. No extra work or spending happens without your written approval. A signed agreement governs each engagement. These principles explain how I work. They don't replace it.
Work with other firms follows the partners standard: who does what is written down before work starts, and any referral fee is disclosed to you.

docs.s: How a neon1 project moves from your problem to a result you can run, step by step.
k: Every project follows the same path, scaled to its size: understand one real task, measure where it stands, compare the options, agree on a bounded result, build it in small steps, teach it, and check later that it helped. The process page is the one-minute version. This is the full one.

I ask for the last finished example, the next one coming, and a recent failure. With your permission I watch the work happen, often over a short screen share. I note who starts it, what information comes in, where it waits, which steps need judgment, and what "done" means. The result is a plain problem statement, such as "When a new request arrives, the receptionist copies it into two places and sometimes misses the requested date." "Build an AI agent" is a solution, not a problem statement. I don't copy private records into my notes just because they were on screen. For personal clients I ask about comfort, accessibility, shared devices, and who will help later, and I'm happy to slow down and write steps out.

Before changing anything I time a few real examples. Hands-on effort and waiting time are measured separately, and so are errors and exceptions. Then we write one sentence on the outcome, one measure of success, and one guardrail. For example: cut retyping time without increasing wrong customer records. Saved minutes don't automatically become money. If we put a dollar value on time, the assumption is written down next to it.

I lay out at least four: improve the process, configure what you already have, adopt a new service, or build something narrow. Each gets its ongoing cost, the effort to learn it, how your data is handled, who maintains it, what happens when it fails, and how you'd leave. "Do nothing for now" is on the list too.

The scope is small enough to demonstrate at handover. It lists the normal cases, what's excluded, what data and accounts you'll provide, who approves, and how we'll check it works. Uncertain work sits behind a paid discovery step or a separate spending cap. See the proposal template . If something new comes up, a change request says what it is, what it costs, how it moves the dates, and how it changes acceptance. Nothing extra happens before you approve it.
Build and test in small steps

You see a basic working version early, using safe sample data, so you can tell me whether it matches your task. Configuration and code are versioned, test and live access are kept apart, and every release records how to roll it back. Checks follow the promise: a valid request arrives once, missing fields are explained, one person can't see another's records, a duplicate doesn't create duplicate work, and an outage leaves a visible, recoverable state. I test on the browsers, devices, and accessibility needs that are in scope, including a slow connection when that's realistic.

I show one ordinary task. You do it. Then you fix a harmless mistake on purpose. Where you hesitate, the instructions get better. The handover covers the workflow, who owns each account, recurring costs, routine steps, common errors, backup and recovery, vendor contacts, support terms, how to export, and known limits. Passwords go in a password manager, never in the handover document. We record acceptance against the agreed checks, and I remove access I no longer need. The release and handover record is the checklist.

At the agreed review date we look at whether the new workflow is being used and whether it fixed the original problem, including any upkeep it added. If something new is needed, it's because of a real need, not to fill a care plan. Permission to do the work isn't permission to publish it. I ask separately before naming you, quoting you, or showing a screenshot.

Method Where it helps What I avoid Kanban and work-in-progress limits Making waiting and unfinished work visible Treating a task board as a management system Plan, do, study, act Testing one change and studying the result Changing things without a prediction Lean waste analysis Removing retyping, waiting, and extra handoffs Removing checks because they look slow Five whys and root cause analysis Understanding a recurring problem Forcing every incident into one cause or one person Failure mode and effects analysis Thinking through failures before a risky release Treating guessed scores as real probabilities A simple responsibility table Who does, approves, and is told Two people both "owning" one decision Architecture decision records Keeping the reason for a big choice A record for every small preference Usability testing Checking the whole task, including recovery Testing only looks or expert use These are tools, not certifications. I use the parts that help and say so when I'm only using some of them.

docs.s: How neon1 uses git: branch names, commit messages, merges, protected branches, and the history rules, and which safeguards production and client data require.
k: Every neon1 project lives in git, on GitHub. These rules apply to all of them. A repository can add stricter rules in its own VCS-ETIQUETTE.md , but not looser ones. The rules get stricter when a repository deploys to production or holds client data, whatever its version number says.

Check which branch you're on, what's staged, and whether anyone else's changes are in the working tree. Keep unrelated changes out. One branch holds one change. Run the project's checks and read the full diff before committing.

Name a branch after the kind of change and what it does, in lowercase words joined by hyphens: Prefix For Example feat/ New capability, documents, or tools feat/knowledge-center fix/ Something wrong: a bug, a wrong fact, a broken link fix/office-hours docs/ Documentation about the project itself docs/vcs-etiquette refactor/ Restructuring that changes no behavior refactor/split-services chore/ CI, dependencies, and housekeeping chore/node-24 release/ Preparing a release release/v1.0.0 If a second problem turns up while working, it gets its own branch.

neon1 follows Conventional Commits 1.0.0 : type(scope): plain summary in lowercase with no period Optional body: why the change was made, when the diff doesn't say. Optional footers, such as BREAKING CHANGE: what breaks and how to move. Types: feat (a new capability), fix (a correction), docs , refactor , test , chore , perf , build , ci . Scope is optional and names the area, such as fix(settings) or feat(templates) . A breaking change gets a ! after the type or scope, such as feat(api)!: , and a BREAKING CHANGE: footer. The summary says what the change does, as an instruction: fix(contact): correct weekday hours , not fixed stuff . Messages follow the writing standard . They're written for someone reading the history a year later.

Commit at a point that makes sense on its own: a finished workflow, a narrow fix, a complete document. Source, tests, and documentation for one change go in the same commit. Every commit on the main branch passes the checks.

Commits are made under the name and email of the person responsible for the change. Tools that help along the way, including AI review tools, aren't listed as authors or co-authors. The person committing has read and stands behind every line.

Merge a feature branch with git merge --no-ff , so the branch stays visible in history, then delete it. Small pull requests may be squash-merged once the repository is protected (see below) when the individual commits don't matter. Keep the main branch releasable. If the checks fail on main, fixing them comes before anything else.

Never rewrite history on the main branch, on a shared branch, or on anyone else's branch. Rebasing your own unpushed work is fine. Never force-push to main. A mistake on main is fixed by a new commit, such as a git revert . A leaked secret is revoked and rotated first. Removing it, or correcting a wrong author, from history is a separate decision the repository's owner makes deliberately, with branch protection paused only for that change and restored right after.

A repository that deploys nothing to production and holds no client data moves fast, and these are strong habits rather than hard gates: Named branches for anything bigger than a typo, merged with --no-ff . Typos and broken links may go straight to main. Pull requests are optional. Read your own diff before merging.
From the first live release, or when client data is at stake

Production deployment and risk to clients or their data decide when the safeguards apply, not the version number. A v0.x repository that deploys a live site or holds client data follows these rules from its first live release: The main branch is protected against force pushes and deletion, with no one allowed to bypass that. Required checks pass before a change reaches main. Every change is reviewed as a full diff before it merges. When a second person is available, someone other than the author approves it. Policies and agreements also need a reviewer who can check them against what's live. Rollback is ready: the previous release can be put back, and how is written down before the release goes out. Signed commits and tags on main, from v1.0.0 on. Urgent fixes , such as a wrong policy or contact detail, go on a fix/urgent-... branch and can be merged with one review and released as a patch the same day. How this works today neon1 is one person, so the controls are honest about that. On the repositories that deploy to production (the website, the 1NEON portal, the chat, and the AWS infrastructure), main has two rulesets in force: No force push or deletion , with no bypass for anyone, including me. Required checks must pass before a change lands on main. As the sole maintainer and repository admin, I can bypass this ruleset, and GitHub prints a bypass warning whenever I push to main directly. That bypass is the sole-maintainer exception. It's for when no second reviewer exists, not for skipping checks. I use it for small changes I've reviewed myself as a full diff, with the checks run locally first, and for an urgent fix when waiting would cause more harm. Each bypass shows in GitHub's warnings and in the history, and I look back at any bypassed change once it's live. When a second maintainer joins, review by someone other than the author becomes required.
Every released version has an annotated tag on the commit it was built from, named exactly vX.Y.Z . Tags are never moved or deleted once pushed. See versioning and releases for when to tag.
Conventional Commits 1.0.0 Pro Git, Git Branching GitHub, About protected branches

docs.s: How neon1 numbers releases of code (vX.Y.Z) and editions of documents (X.Y), when each number goes up, and how tags, changelogs, and package files stay in agreement.
k: A version number tells people what changed and whether they need to do anything about it. That only works if the numbers follow rules. neon1 uses two schemes: one for software and one for documents.

Software follows Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 . A version has three numbers, MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH , and is written with a v in tags and prose, such as v1.4.2 . Number Goes up when Example Major (X) Something that worked before stops working, or people must change how they use it Removing a command, renaming a setting, changing a data format Minor (Y) New capability is added and everything that worked still works A new page, command, report, or option Patch (Z) Something is corrected and nothing new is added A bug fix, a wrong fact, a security fix that changes nothing else When a number goes up, the numbers to its right reset to zero: v1.4.2 then v1.5.0 , never v1.5.2 .

Versions starting with 0 mean initial development. The rules above still guide the numbers, with one change: a breaking change bumps the minor number instead of the major one, because nothing is promised yet. Patch ( v0.4.1 ): fixes only. Minor ( v0.5.0 ): a release with new capability, or a breaking change. A minor number counts releases, not merges or days. Ten small merges that ship together are one release. A version is never a percentage of completeness, so v0.42.0 doesn't mean 42% done. Start at v0.1.0 for the first usable release.

v1.0.0 is the first complete, dependable release of the project's whole intended scope, shown to work for the people it's for, with documentation, recovery, and its known limits written down. From then on, a breaking change means a new major version, and people can rely on the numbers.
A release that's being tested before it's final gets a suffix: v1.0.0-rc.1 , v2.0.0-beta.2 . Pre-releases sort before the final version, and nothing depends on them in production.

A release's number appears in several places, and they must agree: The git tag , annotated, on the exact commit the release was built from. The changelog's top entry. The package file , if the project has one ( package.json , pyproject.toml ). Anything the release shows people, such as a site's footer or a --version flag. A project's checks should fail when these disagree. Every version named in a changelog has a tag, and every tag has a changelog entry. Tags are never moved or reused.

If a project's numbers have drifted, such as a package file saying 0.42.0 while the latest tag is v0.13.0 , don't rewrite old tags. Pick the next correct number from where the project actually is, make every place agree in that release, and note the change in the changelog. History stays as it was, and the numbers are right from then on.
Every project keeps a CHANGELOG.md , newest first, following Keep a Changelog 1.1.0 :

Added What's new, written for the people who use it. Fixed What was wrong and is now right. The release date may follow the version in the heading. Sections are Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, and Security, used only when they have entries. Work merged but not yet released goes under ## Unreleased. Entries follow the [writing standard](writing.md): they describe the change from the reader's side, not the code's.

Merge everything the release includes into main, with the checks passing. Update the changelog and every place the version appears, in one commit. Merge it to main. The pipeline deploys it, checks that what's live reports the new version, and then tags that commit: vX.Y.Z , annotated. A project without a pipeline tags by hand the same way: git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "vX.Y.Z: one line on what it brings" , then pushes the tag.

In every neon1 repository, the pipeline makes the tag, not a person. A tag then always means "this exact commit passed its checks and is live", and a release can't be forgotten or tagged on the wrong commit. Repository Where the version is set When the tag is made neon1-site The changelog, the page's version, and the footer After the deploy, once the live site reports the new version neon1-1NEON The changelog and package.json After the deploy, once the portal is verified live neon1-chat The changelog and package.json After the deploy, once Neo's health check reports the new commit neon1-aws-infrastructure The changelog Once every stack's plan or apply has passed neon1-corpus The changelog On main, by the release workflow, which also publishes the bundles A change that people will notice ships in a release. Add its changelog entry in the same merge: a fix goes under the next patch, new capability under the next minor. A push with no new version ships under the current one. Keep that to changes nobody would notice, such as CI, comments, or a dependency bump with no effect. Checks enforce agreement. Each repository's checks fail when its version places disagree, and the tag step stops when the changelog names no version. A tag that exists is never made again or moved. If a release went wrong, the fix is the next patch.

Documents, such as the standards, policies, and templates in this Knowledge Center, use an edition written as two numbers without a v : 1.0 , 1.1 , 2.0 . The missing v keeps document editions distinct from software versions. Number Goes up when Major (X) A promise, a rule, a required field, or an obligation changes Minor (Y) Wording is clarified, a fact is corrected, or something is added without changing a promise 1.0 is the first edition published as adopted, after an editing pass for accuracy, plain language, and the conventions of its kind. Below 1.0 is a draft. Each document also records when it was first written and when it was last updated, taken from its real history. A collection of documents, such as neon1-corpus, is itself software and follows vX.Y.Z : a new document is a minor release, and a correction is a patch.
Semantic Versioning 2.0.0 Keep a Changelog 1.1.0 Git, Tagging

docs.s: How neon1 code reads: names, comments, file headers, formatting, and layout, in every language and configuration format.
k: Code is read far more often than it's written. These conventions make neon1 code quick to understand for someone who didn't write it. They apply to every language and every format that allows comments, including tests, shell scripts, Dockerfiles, CI workflows, Terraform, and templates. A project's formatter and linter win where they conflict with this page.

Use the shortest name that keeps the meaning clear: retryLimit , not rl or maximumNumberOfRetryAttemptsAllowed . Name things for what they mean to the reader, not how they're built: unpaidInvoices , not filteredList . Use the project's existing words for its concepts. If the interface says "workspace," the code says workspace too. When renaming, rename every use in the same change, and keep public interfaces stable or version the change.

Explain why, not what. A comment gives the purpose, a constraint, an invariant, or a reason that isn't visible in the code. It doesn't narrate the next line. Comment at every semantic junction : section boundaries, exported or public functions, classes, and components, non-obvious invariants, security and tenancy rules, and configuration blocks. Usually one or two lines, without a closing period on single-line comments. Between junctions, code that already says plainly what it does needs no comment of its own. Start with the meaning. Don't repeat the function's name or open with "This function." For example, // Invalid records are rejected before anything is written . Keep comments true. A comment that no longer matches the code is a bug. Update or remove it in the same change. Judge comments by usefulness and truth, not by count. A review asks whether each comment tells a reader something they need and whether it's still accurate. Adding comments to reach a number, or a test that counts them, doesn't make code clearer. Use each language's native documentation format where tools read it: docstrings in Python, doc comments in Go, JSDoc where a project uses it. Document parameters, results, and errors only when they add something the signature doesn't say.

Every source file starts with a one-line header saying what it is and what it's for, after any line that must come first (a shebang, a license, or a directive): #!/usr/bin/env node // tools/export.mjs - Writes the bundle a consumer reads. // Usage: node tools/export.mjs --target chat|site|knowledge|ai The header uses sentence case and a period. The header and junction rules apply to files people write and maintain. See the exceptions below. A Usage: line follows when the file can be run, showing a real invocation without closing punctuation. Full help belongs in --help , not the header.

Let the formatter decide what it can: Prettier, Black, gofmt, terraform fmt . Two blank lines between top-level definitions and major sections, one between related groups inside them. Break long lines at meaningful points, one argument or item per line when a call gets long. Keep a file about one thing. When a file grows a second purpose, split it.

Prefer plain functions and data over frameworks and abstractions until a pattern repeats at least three times. Keep business logic separate from input, output, and presentation, so it can be tested on its own. Validate input where it enters the system, and trust it after that. Fail loudly with a clear message. Never swallow an error silently. Configuration comes from the environment or a config file, never from values hard-coded in several places.

Prefer the platform's built-in features, then small, well-maintained libraries. Pin exact versions in lock files, including CI actions pinned to a commit. Each new dependency needs a reason: what it does that would be costly to write and maintain. Check its license for the way it will be used.

These don't get added headers or comments: Generated files , such as compiled output, generated clients, and build artifacts. Document the generator and its inputs instead, and regenerate rather than editing by hand. Vendored code copied from another project. Leave it as its authors wrote it, and record where it came from and which version in the nearest README or notice file. Lock files , such as package-lock.json or go.sum . Their tools own them. Formats with their own authoritative description , such as a JSON Schema with description fields, an OpenAPI document, or a migration tracked by its tool. The description fields are where the explanation goes.
Strict JSON and similar formats can't hold comments. Don't invent them. Put the explanation in the nearest file that can hold it, such as the README or the code that reads the file.

docs.s: What neon1 tests, how changes are checked and reviewed before they ship, and what done means.
k: Tests and reviews exist to catch the problems that would hurt the people using the work. A large test count isn't the goal. Evidence that the promised behavior works, and fails safely, is.

Tests follow the promise made to the client or user: The main task works end to end. The common failure is handled: missing input, an outage, a timeout. Duplicates and retries don't create duplicate work, such as a second invoice. Permissions hold: one person can't reach another's data, including through exports and search. Recovery works: a backup restores, a deploy rolls back. Accessibility and devices in scope: keyboard, screen reader, phone, and slow connections where they matter. When a bug is found, a test that would have caught it is written first, then the fix.

Check What it catches When it runs Formatting and linting Style drift and simple mistakes Every commit, locally and in CI Unit tests Logic errors in one piece Every commit Integration tests Pieces that don't fit together Every pull request or merge End-to-end and browser tests Broken user paths Before every release Security scans Leaked secrets, known vulnerable dependencies Every push Accessibility checks Missing labels, contrast, keyboard traps Before every release that changes an interface Live checks The deployed version isn't the one built After every deploy Checks run the same way on a laptop and in CI, from one command, such as make check . A check that can't run somewhere says so, rather than passing quietly.

Every change gets read in full before it merges, as a diff, by its author at minimum. Once a repository deploys to production or holds client data, from its first live release and whatever its version number, its required checks must pass and someone other than the author reviews each change when a second person is available. While neon1 is one person, the version control standard describes the sole-maintainer exception. A review asks: Does it do what it says, and only that? Is anything unsafe: secrets, permissions, data loss, irreversible actions? Are the tests about the promise, and do they pass? Is it as simple as it can be? Is it readable, with names and comments that follow the code style ? Are the docs, changelog, and version updated? AI review tools can help find problems. They don't approve changes. A person decides.

A change is done when all of these are true: It does what was agreed, including the failure cases that matter The checks pass, and new behavior has tests The diff has been read in full Docs, changelog, and version are updated It's merged, released, and running where it should be Someone has checked it works there Merged isn't done. Deployed but unchecked isn't done either.

Report what was actually checked and how. Keep the difference between "passes locally," "passes in CI," "deployed," and "confirmed working by the people who use it." When something wasn't checked, say so.

docs.s: The documents every neon1 project keeps, what each one is for, and how they stay true: READMEs, changelogs, decision records, and runbooks.
k: Documentation lets someone use, run, or change a project without asking its author. It's written once, in one place, kept next to the code it describes, and updated in the same change as the code.

File For Contains README.md Anyone arriving at the project What it is, who it's for, its status, how to run, test, and deploy it, and its license CHANGELOG.md People using it What changed in each release, newest first. See versioning LICENSE Anyone reusing it The license text, plus NOTICE when required SECURITY.md Anyone who finds a problem How to report it privately. See the security disclosure policy Larger projects add: File For Contains VCS-ETIQUETTE.md or CONTRIBUTING.md Contributors Any rules stricter than the version control standard Decision records Future maintainers Why a significant choice was made, the options considered, and what would change it Runbooks Whoever operates it Step-by-step tasks such as deploy, roll back, restore, and rotate a secret

Following Diátaxis , each document does one of four jobs, and doesn't mix them: Tutorial: learning by doing, for a newcomer. How-to: steps to finish a specific task. Reference: exact facts to look up, such as commands, settings, and fields. Explanation: why things are the way they are. A README usually holds a short version of each and links out when one grows.

Write one when a choice is costly to reverse: a database, a framework, a hosting model, a license. Keep it to a page: the context, the decision, the options rejected and why, and what would make us revisit it. Number them and never delete one. A changed decision gets a new record that replaces the old one. The tool and architecture decision form is a template.

Prerequisites come first, then commands in the order they're run, each with what you should see and what to do if you don't. Commands are copied exactly and tested. A runbook nobody has followed is a draft.

Docs change in the same commit as the behavior they describe. A checked fact beats a remembered one. Commands in a README should be run before a release. One source for each fact. Link to it instead of copying it, so it can't drift. That's why neon1's public words live once, in neon1-corpus .

docs.s: How neon1 handles your accounts, access, and information, and the baseline every project starts from.
k: Security work protects your actual task, your information, and your way back when something goes wrong. It starts with who owns what and who can get in, then adds controls to match the data and what's at stake. Installing a tool or running a scan doesn't make a system secure, so I never describe it that way.
Frameworks, used for what they're for

Framework What I use it for NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 Spotting missing responsibilities across Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover CIS Controls, Implementation Group 1 A prioritized starting point for basic hygiene OWASP ASVS Testable requirements for applications, cited by version and number NIST Secure Software Development Framework How software gets built and released safely Informed by a framework isn't the same as certified against it. I won't call work "NIST certified," "compliant," or "enterprise grade" because these sources shaped it.

Before connecting anything, we list the information involved, why it's needed, where it lives, who can see it, which vendors receive it, and when it should be deleted. We label it in plain words: public, internal, confidential, or restricted. I don't collect what the work doesn't need. Development uses sample or redacted records. Before your data goes to a vendor, I explain where it's processed, how long it's kept, and who else touches it. Free consumer accounts and business accounts often have different terms, so I check which one applies. Information also lingers in places people forget: email notifications, automation history, logs, AI prompts, search indexes, and backups. I won't promise complete deletion until I know how each of those behaves.

Named accounts, the least access the job needs, and separate admin roles. Multi-factor sign-in on business and admin accounts, phishing-resistant where the service supports it. No shared admin passwords, and no credentials in proposals, chat, code, or bookmarks. Every grant of access records who approved it, why, and when it ends. After handover I remove what I no longer need and check that it's gone. No remote-control software left installed without a support agreement and your informed consent. For apps with more than one user, I test permissions on the server. Hiding a button doesn't stop a direct request, so I check that one customer can't reach another's records by changing an ID, including through exports and search.

For each project I sketch what's being built, where information changes hands, what could go wrong, and how we'll check. For an intake form that might mean a forged submission, a stolen account, a malicious attachment, or an email sent to the wrong person. Each risk ends with a decision and a test.

Area Practice Evidence kept Inventory Systems, accounts, vendors, data, and owners are named A dated inventory, unknowns included Sign-in Multi-factor sign-in and protected recovery Configuration evidence, never the codes Permissions Least access, with tests that someone can't get in Role table and test results Devices Supported software, updates, disk encryption A device baseline and update record Storage and transfer Encryption, retention, and access that fit the data A data-flow record Secrets Kept out of code, rotated when exposed An inventory by name, never the values Backup Recovery that doesn't share the original's weak points A restore test Logging Important actions logged without sensitive content Sample redacted events Vulnerabilities Findings triaged and fixes rechecked Finding, decision, fix, recheck Changes Big changes reviewed, with a way back Version, approval, and release record Incidents Contacts, authority, and a fallback are written down A current incident procedure This is neon1's starting point, not a full copy of any standard and not a guarantee against compromise. When the stakes call for it, I bring in a specialist.

Code follows the development standard. When a secret leaks, I revoke or rotate it and confirm the old one no longer works. Deleting the visible copy isn't enough. A scan against a live system can change data, so its scope is agreed first.

I ask whether the affected part is actually present, whether the weakness can be reached, whether it's being exploited, and what it would expose. A severity score helps sort the list but doesn't describe your risk. If something urgent needs a faster response than I can give, we arrange someone who can before I take on the service.

What neon1 promises and what a vendor promises are kept apart. The right agreements for your data and location are in place before work starts, such as a business associate agreement when health information is involved. A vendor's compliance badge doesn't cover a custom setup or how I handle the data. Real customer information never appears in a public demo, forum post, or code issue. Screenshots, file names, and logs are scrubbed, and so are document comments and revision history.

Access is right, normal and failure paths behave as agreed, security findings are fixed or knowingly accepted, recovery is believable, recurring charges are understood, and you can run it. We write down who decided and on what evidence. If something important is unknown, we name it and either resolve it or limit the release.

docs.s: How neon1 designs interfaces and documents for any device and for people using assistive technology.
k: Good design means people can do what they came to do quickly, and recover when something goes wrong. neon1 has its own look, but the task comes first.

Every screen and document answers three questions before anything else: what is this, what can I do here, and what happens next. Navigation is ordinary and visible. Nobody has to learn a metaphor, finish an animation, or know a film reference to get to the useful part.

I aim for WCAG 2.2 level AA. That means designing and checking for: Semantic headings and landmarks, so screen readers can jump around. Every control is reachable and usable with a keyboard, with a visible focus ring. Labels on every form field, and errors that say what went wrong and how to fix it. Text contrast that meets AA on every background, including over animation. Targets large enough to tap, at least 44 by 44 pixels for primary controls. Motion that can be paused, and a calm version for people who set their device to reduce motion. Pages that work when zoomed to 200% and on a 320-pixel-wide phone without sideways scrolling. An automated accessibility score is a starting point. I also check with a keyboard, a screen reader, and a phone.

Pages load what they need and nothing else: no trackers, no ad scripts, and no fonts loaded from someone else's server. Images are sized for the screen, and pages should still work on a slow connection.

Short forms, one question per field, and only the questions the task needs. Inputs use the right keyboard on phones. A submitted form says it was received and what happens next. Nothing is lost if a field is wrong.

Documents use one clear column, real headings, comfortable spacing, and tables only for real comparisons. PDFs from the Knowledge Center are tagged for screen readers and carry their title and edition.
The neon1 look, used with restraint

Dark Matrix green over black for personality, light paper and brand green #035704 for reading. Inter for text, JetBrains Mono for labels and code, Aptos in Office documents. The rain animation is decoration. It pauses on request, stops when the tab is hidden, and becomes a still image for reduced motion. Easter eggs, like the white rabbit, are optional and never stand between you and the content. The logo isn't redrawn, stretched, or recolored. neon1 is always lowercase, and the company is neon1 LLC.
The same standard applies to anything I build for you. If something in scope can't meet it, such as a vendor's checkout page we can't change, I'll tell you and note it in the handover.

docs.s: How neon1 chooses tools and architecture, counts the full cost, and checks licenses.
k: I choose technology by your task and by what it costs to run after I've handed it over. Being popular, new, or free isn't a reason on its own.
Start with what you already have

First I list the subscriptions, devices, skills, data, and integrations you already have, and check what's built in. A feature already included in Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace is often cheaper and easier to support than a new free server. For a decision that matters, I compare four options: improve the process, configure an existing product, adopt a managed service, or build a narrow piece. "Not yet" is an option too. Each recommendation says what evidence would change it.

A tool that can't meet the hard requirements is out, however good it looks. Those requirements are permissions, export, lawful use, and recovery. Only then do I compare ease of use, maintenance, total cost, fit, and how good the evidence is. A weighted score helps us talk it through. It isn't an objective fact. The tool and architecture decision form keeps it short.

First-year cost includes setup, subscriptions, computing, storage, data transfer, backups, monitoring, AI usage, payment fees, migration, training, upkeep, and the cost of leaving later. Why the license price isn't the price A free tool on a $12 a month server that needs an hour of someone's time each month, valued here at $75, costs at least $1,044 a year before setup, backups, or incidents. A $25 a month managed service costs $300 a year in fees before its own admin time and limits. Neither is automatically better, and the license price is only part of the cost. I follow the FinOps idea at a small scale: a budget, an owner, a regular look at the bill, and a cost per useful result.
Architecture that fits a small business

A brochure website is usually a static site on managed hosting with versioned source and a documented redeploy. Client workflows use a few clearly owned parts and supported integrations. A modular app or a managed workflow usually beats microservices or Kubernetes at this size. Infrastructure as code is worth it when repeatability and recovery justify the setup. The AWS Well-Architected pillars (operations, security, reliability, performance, cost, sustainability) are a useful lens even when nothing runs on AWS.

Supported APIs over screen scraping. API limits, paging, time zones, currencies, and ID formats written down. Incoming data validated. Each business action gets a stable ID, so a retry doesn't send a second invoice or make a second booking. Temporary failures retry a limited number of times with a delay. Permanent ones go somewhere a person will see them. Partial success is kept. If a record saves but its email fails, the record stays and the failed email shows up. Reconciliation checks make missing or duplicate results visible.

Every service starts with a health check on the journey that matters, a clear failure log, cost visibility, and a named person for alerts. Alerts say what's affected, what to do next, and where the instructions are. A monitor hosted on the same server as the app goes down with it, so it can't report that outage.

Open source, source available, open core, free tier, and free trial mean different things. Code licenses, hosted terms, model weights, datasets, plugins, logos, and fonts can each have their own rules. I read the actual license at the version being adopted, and note whether we're consulting on your own installation, distributing software, embedding it, or hosting it for others. Some popular automation and AI platforms allow internal use but need commercial terms for hosting or white-labeling. Notices and attribution are kept intact.
Qualifying a tool before you rely on it

Confirm it's maintained, the current release, known limits, how security issues are reported, and the license for your use. Read the install, upgrade, export, backup, and recovery docs. Test one real task with sample or approved data somewhere isolated. Test a failure, an access attempt that should fail, an export, and a restore. Measure setup effort, upkeep, ongoing cost, and how easily you can use it. Record the evidence and gaps, then adopt, keep testing, defer, or reject. Name the owner, update policy, review date, and exit before it goes live. Lots of stars or a recent commit isn't enough. A mature project can change rarely, and a busy one can be unstable.

docs.s: How neon1 sets service targets, plans for failure, and tests that backups restore.
k: Reliability means you can do the task when you need to, and get back on your feet when something goes wrong. Targets come from how much interruption and data loss your business can actually tolerate, what the design can do, what it costs, and who's available to respond. I don't start by picking an uptime percentage.

A service profile names the task that matters, operating hours, users, normal volume, dependencies, data owner, support owner, and the manual fallback. "The website" is too vague when the real task is "a request reaches the right person." We describe normal, degraded, and failed states separately, because a form that accepts a request but sends the email late hasn't lost the request. Dependencies such as sign-in, email delivery, payments, and your own internet connection are listed, with which failures the design survives.

Term Meaning SLI (service level indicator) What we observe, such as the share of valid requests stored and acknowledged within a set time SLO (service level objective) The target value for that indicator over a stated window SLA (service level agreement) A contractual promise with consequences. An internal target isn't automatically one Response time Time to a real person's first useful reply, separate from time to fix RTO (recovery time objective) The intended longest time to restore the service after a defined disruption RPO (recovery point objective) How much recent data you can afford to lose, measured in time Definitions follow Google's SRE guidance and NIST SP 800-34 .

Availability target Allowed downtime in 30 days 99% 7 hours 12 minutes 99.5% 3 hours 36 minutes 99.9% 43 minutes 99.99% 4 minutes Each extra nine needs faster detection, faster response, and usually more money. A person who's unavailable until the weekend can't meet 99.9% for anything that needs a human to fix it. So I don't sell targets that the coverage can't back up.

I ask what happens if the task fails for five minutes, an hour, a day, and a weekend. When's the busy period? Is a manual process acceptable, and for how long? Then we price the design and the coverage against those answers. Targets start few, get a baseline period, and say what happens when they're missed.
Recoverable data is more than a schedule

An hourly backup doesn't guarantee an hour of data loss at most. Jobs fail, copies come out incomplete, credentials get lost, and corruption is found late. Recovery also needs uploaded files, configuration, and the keys to decrypt it all. Counting data loss Trouble starts at 10:15. The last backup finished at 9:00, but the data in it only goes up to 8:30. You've lost an hour and forty-five minutes of work, not an hour and fifteen. Replication copies deletions and corruption too, and file sync spreads unwanted changes. I keep an independent copy that matches the threat, following the 3-2-1 idea (several copies, different places, one off site) plus an offline or locked copy and regular test restores, as CISA recommends .

Situation The question How neon1 fits A brochure site with nothing unique stored Can versioned source and a documented deploy rebuild it? A good fit Ordinary intake with a workable manual fallback Can you keep taking requests and catch up afterward? A fit when ownership, backup, and support terms are explicit Essential daily data How much loss and downtime before real harm? Needs proven recovery and coverage beyond appointment-based help Continuous payments or critical operations Who responds right away? I refer you to a provider with the right operations team

Pick a safe, separate destination and a scenario, such as losing the main database or the admin account. Confirm it won't touch the live system or contact real customers. Start the clock at the agreed disruption point. Get the backup and keys through the documented route, then restore data and configuration. Check counts, key records, permissions, and a few real tasks. A success message alone isn't enough. Measure the actual recovery point and the full elapsed time, and note every manual step. You confirm the restored result is usable. Clean up the test copy, update the instructions, and schedule the next test. Restores are tested before handover, after a big change, and at an interval we agree on.

An incident disrupts or threatens normal work. A request asks for access, advice, or a change. Severity comes from the consequences to you. For each incident we name who coordinates, who can change the system, and your contact, and keep a timestamped log. Updates say what's affected, what's known, what isn't, what you can do meanwhile, and when the next update comes. Suspected security incidents follow your agreed route, keep the evidence intact, and bring in the right specialist or insurer. Afterward, a short review covers what happened and what changes, focused on conditions rather than blame.

Ongoing care with neon1 is scheduled attention to a named workflow within an agreed allowance. It isn't a help desk, round-the-clock security monitoring, an unlimited repair fund, or insurance against vendor outages. If the work regularly outgrows the allowance, we change the scope or the price.

docs.s: When neon1 uses AI, how it's tested before anyone relies on it, and where a person stays in charge.
k: I use AI when it makes a defined task better after counting the errors, the review time, privacy, cost, and upkeep. A smooth demo is useful for exploring. It doesn't show that something is dependable. So I start with AI that a person can check and correct, and earn more autonomy with evidence.
Whether AI belongs in the solution

I compare the current process, a simple rule or search, an existing product, and a narrow AI approach. Ordinary software wins when the rules are clear and mistakes are costly. AI tends to help with drafting, sorting messy text, summarizing documents you're allowed to share, and finding the right passage. You still need to know when to double-check. I use the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and its generative AI profile as prompts for who's responsible, what the task is, how it's tested, and what risk is left. They don't certify anything.

Before choosing a model we write down the user, the task, the approved data, the output, the actions it may take, the decisions it may not make, who reviews, and the fallback. We also decide whether the output is a draft, a search aid, a recommendation, or an action, since each needs different checks. A document-search assistant can find an invoice or a policy passage. That doesn't make it fit to give accounting or legal conclusions, and the interface should make that plain. We also set a spending limit, a response time, and how much review effort is acceptable.
A test set that looks like the real work

We collect permitted examples and write the expected answer before tuning anything. The set includes ordinary requests, vague ones, missing information, out-of-date documents, conflicting sources, odd formats, and cases that should be refused or sent to a person. Examples used for building stay separate from examples used for the final check. Twenty or thirty cases are enough to find early problems, but not enough to support a broad reliability claim.

Correctness, evidence, access boundaries, refusals, actions, speed, cost, and human effort are checked separately, and the same cases run against the old way. For search-based assistants I look at what was retrieved and what was claimed, because a plausible citation isn't proof. For data extraction I check fields, units, dates, amounts, and IDs against rules. For classification I look at results per category, since an overall score can hide failure on the rare ones that matter. Evaluation tools that use another model as the judge get checked against a small set graded by a person.

Access is enforced by the application and the search layer, never by a prompt asking the model to behave. Retrieved documents, emails, web pages, and tool output are treated as untrusted input, since prompt injection is a real risk even with retrieval. Tools start read-only. Sending messages, spending money, changing permissions, or deleting anything needs a person to review the actual recipient, content, or change first. An approve button doesn't protect much if you can't see what it approves. Run time, retries, output size, and spend all have limits.

Offline. Tested on permitted examples, away from live data. Shadow. Runs alongside the normal process without changing anything, so we can compare. Assisted pilot. Named people use the output on a limited task, with a fallback and a way to report problems. Controlled use. Expanded only when you accept the evidence, the remaining risks, and the running cost. Some services are best left at the assisted stage permanently. A pilot doesn't have to become autonomous.

Release is blocked by a serious unauthorized disclosure or action in testing, unresolved serious errors, no working recovery, or costs and review effort that cancel the benefit. There's always a way to switch the AI part off and keep doing the essential task by hand or with something simpler.

We track task success, corrections, review minutes, cost per successful task, and speed, and look for groups the change might be failing. Any change to the model, prompt, documents, or tool permissions means rerunning the test set. A provider's benchmark doesn't tell us how it does on your documents.

Only scoped statements with their conditions: "In a twenty-case test using made-up records, it completed eighteen without correction," if that's what happened. Never "reliable AI for every business." Neo, the chat on this site, answers only from neon1's public documents, is run against a set of test questions before each change, and has its directives published in the corpus .

docs.s: How neon1 defines success with you, measures it, and reports what the numbers can and can't show.
k: Measurement shows whether the work was worth it. It starts during discovery with a baseline, gets checked at handover, and gets reviewed after real use. I keep the list short, define every number exactly, and say plainly what a small sample can't prove.

Term Meaning Measurement One observation, such as 18 completed requests Metric A defined way to measure, such as completed requests divided by valid attempts KPI A metric chosen because it matters to an ongoing goal. "Key" should keep the list short Baseline Where things stood before, under stated conditions Target The result we're aiming for Guardrail Something that must not get worse while we improve the main result OKR An objective plus a few measurable key results by a date Publishing a page is a task. People understanding it and acting on it is an outcome. I try to measure outcomes.

Each measure we agree on gets a metric record : what decision it supports, exactly what counts, the formula, the source, the baseline, the target, and the review date. A zero in the denominator means "no data," not zero percent and not perfect. Missing data stays visible as unknown.

Measure Definition Watch out for Task completion Finished tasks ÷ valid attempts A page loading isn't a completed booking First time right Cases needing no correction ÷ completed cases Say how long corrections are watched for Hands-on time Time a person actively works a case Keep it apart from waiting, and include new review time End-to-end time Finish time minus valid request time Include queues and handoffs Net time saved Old effort minus new effort minus new review and upkeep Compare like with like, and don't count saved time twice Error rate Cases with a defined error ÷ cases checked State severity and how you checked Adoption People or cases using the new way ÷ those eligible Forced use isn't satisfaction Independent success People finishing without help ÷ people trying With a few people, it's qualitative evidence Benefit realized Observed benefit ÷ estimated benefit, same period Keep time, money, and quality apart unless the conversion is written down Satisfaction scores such as CSAT and NPS have their place. With a handful of clients, a direct conversation about what worked and what's still hard usually tells us more.

Counts appear next to percentages. Four out of five is 80%, and one more case changes it a lot. Failed and abandoned cases stay in the data. A survey only happy customers answer overstates satisfaction. Zero failures in 20 representative trials still allows a failure rate near 14% at 95% confidence. A small pilot finds problems. It can't prove near-perfection. (The math follows NIST's handbook .) Seasons, staff changes, and training also move numbers, so before-and-after reports name them. I don't claim cause and effect without a design that could show it.
What a report from me looks like

One page when possible: the result you wanted, the period and sample size, the baseline, what we see now, cost and effort, failures and exceptions, what the numbers can't establish, and the next decision. Quotes appear only with permission. The question it answers is whether the change is worth keeping.

For software I track how often changes ship, how long they take, how often they fail, and how fast service comes back. For websites I check Core Web Vitals and test accessibility against WCAG 2.2 AA on the real pages. An automated accessibility score is a starting point, not a certificate.

docs.s: Who neon1 works with, how the work differs from households to enterprises, and when it declines work.
k: Some things stay the same for every customer: I listen first, say plainly what I can and can't do, keep you in control of what you own, and leave you able to run it. The shape of the work changes with the kind of customer.

No shaming an old spreadsheet, a cheap tool, or anyone's comfort level with technology. You see the task done, then you do it, then you fix a harmless mistake yourself. Monitoring, recording, AI use, and data access are always visible. Efficiency never becomes hidden surveillance of your staff. "Do nothing," "use the support you already have," and "hire a specialist" are always on the table. Your accounts, data, and documents stay yours, with a clean way out.

Home networks, cameras, devices, passwords, and security habits for families. I write steps in plain words, slow down when asked, and think about who will help when I'm not there. Embarrassment about technology is never a sales tactic. For older relatives, a printed one-page guide often beats an app.

My main focus. Owner-run service businesses, offices, and practices where the same information gets typed into several places, nobody quite understands the setup, or the person who knew how it worked has left. A first engagement is usually a paid review or one workflow, small enough to finish and check in a few weeks. I talk with both the owner who pays and the person who does the work.

Startups and technical small businesses that need clearer cloud accounts, deployments they can trust, infrastructure as code, AI assistants grounded in their own documents, or SOC 2 readiness. Here I work inside your repositories and processes, follow your conventions, and document decisions as I go. Your team owns the result and can keep going without me.

As a one-person practice, I fit best on a focused piece of a larger effort, such as a proof of concept, a review, an automation, or training, alongside your own teams. I'll follow your security, procurement, and change processes. I won't take on round-the-clock operations, large migrations that need a team, or formal assurance. The alternatives page lists who's better placed for those.
Health care and other regulated work

When a project touches health information, a business associate agreement is signed before any access, and the work is designed to use as little sensitive data as possible. I don't make clinical, legal, or financial judgments, and I don't build systems that make them unattended.

I'll turn down or refer work that needs emergency coverage, safety-critical equipment, regulated professional judgment, hidden employee monitoring, or anything I can't support properly. I'll also say no when what you need is simpler than what you asked for, and point you to the simpler thing.
Separately from paid work, I set aside a little time each month to help people and groups in my community, chosen at my discretion. It isn't used to sell paid work.

docs.s: How neon1 works with other firms, vendors, and referrals, and how responsibilities and fees are disclosed.
k: Some projects need another firm, a vendor, or a specialist alongside me. That works when everyone knows who's responsible for what, and causes problems when an introduction turns into an assumed obligation. These rules keep responsibilities written down.

A partner responsibilities sheet is filled in and shared with the client. It names who sells, builds, supports, invoices, sees the data, owns the deliverables, and carries insurance, and what happens if the work ends.

If I'd receive a referral fee or any other benefit for recommending a vendor or firm, you'll know before you decide. I don't recommend tools because of affiliate programs. When a free or built-in option fits, I recommend it.

Working with an AWS Partner, Microsoft partner, or any other program member doesn't make neon1 one. A certification I hold personally doesn't certify the business. Building on a platform doesn't imply the platform endorses the work. Before naming a relationship or using a partner's logo, I check that the relationship is current and that I'm allowed to.

Vendors bill you directly when possible, under your account, so you keep the relationship and the data if neon1 steps away. I read vendor terms for data handling, export, and pricing changes before recommending them, and I tell you what I found.
I don't hand your work or your data to anyone else without your written approval. When health information is involved, any subcontractor signs the same business associate terms first.
When someone else is better placed, I refer you to them, with no fee or obligation attached.
Other firms are welcome to send me work that fits, such as a small business workflow or a security awareness session. The same rules apply in both directions.

docs.s: How neon1 finds clients and talks about its work, and the sales tactics it doesn't use.
k: Selling, for neon1, means helping you decide quickly whether I'm the right help, and telling you when I'm not.
What I make clear, in order

Recognition. Your problem, described in ordinary words. Fit. Who the offer is for, and when it isn't. Credibility. Who does the work (me) and real examples, labeled honestly. Clarity on cost. The paid next step, what affects the price, and recurring costs, in the proposal before anything starts. Control. How you approve work, what you own, how to cancel, and what the handover includes. Reliability. When I respond, how failures are handled, and what support isn't included.

Fake scarcity, countdowns, or "only two spots left" unless it's literally true and relevant. Shame or fear, including the fear of being "left behind" by AI. Fabricated reviews, logos, client lists, or numbers. Guilt-trip exit messages or hard-to-cancel subscriptions. Cold email lists bought from someone else. Contact comes from people who asked, referrals, and my own network. Tracking you around the internet. The website has no ads, analytics, or trackers.

You ask I answer "That's expensive." We check the value against the budget. I can offer a smaller useful step, not the same work for half the price. "Why not do it ourselves?" Often you can. I'll say which parts, and what review, testing, and training would add. "We need someone during the day." Then I may not be the right fit, and I'll help you find the coverage you need. "Can you guarantee the savings?" I commit to deliverables and to measuring the result. Estimates are labeled as estimates. "Will we depend on you?" You'll own the accounts, have the instructions and exports, and know how to leave.

Every public claim has a record behind it: the wording, what supports it, its scope, the date, permission, and its limits. A case study states the problem, my role, what was delivered, how it was checked, the result, and what's still unknown. A clear result without a number beats an invented percentage. Work I did as an employee can show my background, but it isn't presented as neon1's client work. Testimonials reflect the person's real experience, disclose relationships such as family, and never put a technical guarantee in a client's mouth, following the FTC's guidance . Experiments are labeled as experiments.
Local relationships and referrals, LinkedIn, GitHub, and this website. What I publish, including the Knowledge Center, is meant to be useful to anyone who reads it.
One follow-up after a proposal, then the next move is yours. If you say no, that's the end of it, and you're welcome back anytime.

docs.s: How a small office or household checks that its backups would restore what it needs.
k: Until you've restored from a backup, you don't know whether it works. This guide helps you find out before you need it.

Make a short list of what would hurt to lose: Documents and shared folders Email Accounting, customer, or patient records Photos Settings and passwords for important systems Next to each, write down how much recent work you could afford to lose, an hour, a day, or a week, and how long you could manage without it.

3 copies of anything important: the original plus two backups. 2 different kinds of storage , such as a cloud service and an external drive. 1 copy away from the building , so a fire or theft doesn't take everything. Add one more: at least one copy that ransomware can't reach, either offline (a drive you unplug) or a cloud backup with version history that can't be deleted quickly.

Services like Dropbox, OneDrive, and iCloud Drive keep files the same everywhere. That means a deleted or scrambled file is deleted or scrambled everywhere too. Their version history helps, but only for as long as they keep it. Check how long that is.

Pick a quiet time and try it: Choose a file from last week and restore it to a different folder Open it and check it's the right version and not damaged Restore something larger, such as a whole folder or a mailbox Time how long it takes Check you can do it without the person who set it up Write down what happened, especially anything that was confusing or slow.

Check that backups are still running once a month. Most tools send a report or show a last-backup date. Do a test restore every few months, and after any big change. Keep the instructions somewhere you can reach if your main computer is the thing that failed. Make sure more than one person knows how to get the data back. A backup review is one of the smallest projects I take on. The instructions are yours either way.

docs.t: Before you buy a new tool
docs.s: Ten questions to ask before adding software to your business, so it fits, lasts, and lets you leave.
k: New software can fix a problem or add a new one. These questions take about ten minutes.
1. Can something you already pay for do it?
Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, your accounting software, and your point of sale often have forms, automation, booking, or reports built in. Check first.
Write one sentence: "When X happens, we currently do Y, and Z goes wrong." If you can't, the tool can't either.
3. Who will use it every day?
Ask them. A tool the staff avoid won't fix the problem, however much the owner likes it.
4. What does it cost per year, all in?
Subscription per user, add-ons, payment fees, setup, training, and the hours someone will spend looking after it. Free trials end, and introductory prices rise.
5. Can you get your data out?
Look for an export to a standard format, such as CSV or PDF. Try it during the trial. If leaving is hard, that's a cost.
The account should be in your business's name, billed to you, with at least two people who can get in. Not a contractor's personal account.
Where it's stored, who at the company can see it, how long it's kept, and whether it's used to train AI. For health information, ask whether they'll sign a business associate agreement.
Is there a way to keep working by hand for a day? Who do you contact, and when do they answer?
9. Does it connect to what you have?
Look for a built-in integration or an official API, rather than copying data by hand or a fragile workaround.
10. What will tell you it worked?
Pick one thing to measure before you start, such as time spent, errors, or missed requests, and check it again in a month.
If 1, 5, or 6 has a bad answer, wait. If they're fine and 2 and 3 are clear, try it on one small piece of work first. The tool decision form is the longer version I use with clients.

docs.t: Do you need a business associate agreement?
docs.s: A plain guide for health practices on when a vendor needs a BAA, and what to check before signing one.
k: General information, not legal advice This guide explains the idea in plain words. Your privacy officer or counsel makes the call for your practice. Under HIPAA, a health practice can share patient information with a vendor that does work on its behalf only if the vendor signs a business associate agreement (BAA) first. The agreement says how the vendor will protect the information and what it will do if something goes wrong.

You need a BAA with a vendor when both are true: Your practice is a covered entity, such as a provider that bills insurance electronically, a health plan, or a clearinghouse The vendor creates, receives, keeps, or sends patient information for you Common examples: your practice management or electronic health record system, a billing service, a cloud storage or email provider holding patient messages, an IT consultant who works inside those systems, and a transcription service.

A vendor that never touches patient information, such as someone fixing your printer with no access to records Your internet provider just carrying data, without storing it Other providers you share information with for treatment, who have their own HIPAA duties

Is patient information needed at all? Often the work can be done with made-up or de-identified data instead. What's the smallest amount needed? Ask the vendor to name it. How fast will they report a problem? Look for a specific number of days. Who else will see it? Subcontractors must agree to the same terms. What happens at the end? The data should be returned or destroyed, and confirmed in writing. Do their own tools have BAAs? If they put your data into another service, such as an AI tool or a form builder, that service needs one too.

Many projects never touch patient information, and I design them that way when I can. When one does, we go through the BAA request together first, and the agreement is signed before any access. You can read neon1's example agreement and a filled-out request for a fictional practice.

docs.t: Getting ready for a first call
docs.s: What to bring to a free 15-minute call with neon1.
k: The first call is free and short, about 15 minutes. Its job is to find the main pain point and whether I'm the right help. A little preparation helps.
The most useful thing to bring is the last time the problem happened. Not "our intake is messy," but "on Tuesday a referral sat in the inbox for three days." Real examples show where the work waits.

What happens, step by step, from start to finish? How often does it happen, and roughly how long does it take? What goes wrong, and what do people do when it does? What must not change, such as a system you're keeping or a way customers reach you? What would "fixed" look like to you? You don't need exact numbers. "About 40 a week, maybe 5 minutes each" is plenty.

A list of the tools and subscriptions involved Who owns or administers each account Who else should be part of the conversation, especially the person who does the work every day Please don't send passwords, health details, or payment information, before the call or during it. If the work involves health information, we'll go through the business associate agreement request before any access.

A plain description of the problem A few options, including doing nothing and using what you already have Whether I'm a good fit, and if not, who might be The smallest useful next step, if there is one After the call, you'll get a short proposal with options and estimates if it makes sense. Nothing starts until you pick one. The intake form is what I fill in from our conversation. Book a call or see contact for other ways to reach me.

docs.t: A password manager for your family
docs.s: How to move a household onto a password manager, step by step, without locking anyone out.
k: A password manager remembers a different strong password for every account, so nobody has to reuse one. Reused passwords are one of the most common ways accounts get taken over. Here's how to set one up for a household without anyone getting locked out.

Choose a well-known manager with family sharing and apps for every device you use. Many good ones exist, including the ones built into Apple and Google devices. Pick the one everyone in the household will use. Recovery works differently in each one, and in most of them it only works if it was set up before anything went wrong. Before you move important accounts, read the recovery section for the one you picked.

Decide who will be the family organizer Pick a time when everyone has their phone and computer nearby Have a pen and paper ready for the recovery details Know which product and plan you're using, and which recovery options it offers on that plan Make sure each person can get into the email address and phone number their account uses for recovery, on their own

The organizer creates the family account and sets a long master password: four or five random words are easy to remember and hard to guess. Turn on two-step sign-in for the password manager itself. Set up recovery now, the way your product does it (see recovery by product ), and write down anything it gives you on paper. Keep it somewhere safe at home, such as with other important papers. This is the one thing to protect most. Invite each family member. Each person gets their own vault and master password. Shared things, like streaming and Wi-Fi, go in a shared vault. Install it on every device , then turn on autofill in the phone's settings.

Start with email, banking, and the phone carrier. These are the accounts that can reset everything else. For each one: Sign in with the old password. Let the manager generate a new one and save it. Turn on two-step sign-in while you're there. Do the rest over the following weeks, whenever each account comes up. There's no need to change everything in one evening.

Keep it to one device at first. Show it, then let them do it, then let them fix a mistake on purpose. Leave a one-page printed guide with the three things they'll do most: open the manager, find a password, and fill it in. If your product has a trusted contact or family recovery feature, set it up now so a family member can help if they get stuck.

Reviewed 2026-11-10. Each product changes its options over time, so follow its own instructions, linked below, rather than this summary. In every case, recovery may be impossible if nothing was set up beforehand. Don't try a recovery just to test it: some steps reset your password or keys, or can't be undone. Instead, check that what you set up is still in place. Apple Passwords and iCloud Keychain Your passwords are tied to your Apple Account, so recovering them means recovering that account. Apple offers a recovery contact , a trusted person who can help you get a code, and an optional recovery key . If you turn on a recovery key and later can't provide it, Apple says you can be locked out permanently, and Apple can't give it back to you. Don't store the key in the Passwords app itself. Google Password Manager Your passwords are tied to your Google Account. By default you get them back on a new device by signing in with your Google password, so keep your Google recovery phone and email current. If you turned on on-device encryption , Google says losing every recovery option (your Google password, an eligible device's screen lock, and every signed-in device) can mean losing the saved passwords. Bitwarden Bitwarden can't reset or recover a forgotten master password . Recovery only works through something set up in advance, such as a password hint, a device that's still signed in, a login passkey, or emergency access. If none of those work, the vault can't be recovered. Emergency access has to be set up before it's needed, and the person granting it needs a paid plan (Premium, or a paid organization such as Families). The trusted contact can use a free account. 1Password Sign-in uses your account password together with a Secret Key, which is printed on your Emergency Kit. The Secret Key isn't a recovery method: you need it to sign in on a new device. Separately, you can generate a recovery code on individual and family accounts and keep it safe; it lets you recover your own account with access to your email, and it doesn't exist until you create it. In a family account, the family organizer can also recover a member's account. After either kind of recovery you get a new Secret Key, so save the new Emergency Kit.

Forgot the master password: follow your product's own recovery steps from recovery by product , using what you set up in step 3. Lost a phone: sign in on another device and remove the lost one from the account. A site says the password is wrong: check that you're on the real site, not a look-alike from a link in an email.

docs.t: Use case: a cloud account you can trust
docs.s: How a typical cloud engineering engagement goes for a small technical team: inventory, infrastructure as code, deploys, and tested recovery.
k: A typical pattern, not a client story This page describes how this kind of work usually goes. For real projects, see the case studies . Use case: a cloud account you can trust

A small team's cloud account grew by hand. Nobody is quite sure what every resource is for, who can change what, or what the bill pays for. Deploys work, mostly, from one person's laptop. Backups exist, probably.

Inventory. Every account, resource, role, and recurring cost listed with an owner, plus the unknowns. Access first. Named accounts, multi-factor sign-in, least privilege, and no long-lived keys on laptops. Infrastructure as code. The important resources are imported into Terraform and reviewed like code, so the account can be rebuilt and changes leave a record. Deploys from CI. Short-lived credentials, checks before every deploy, a version you can verify live, and a known rollback. Recovery, proven. The data that matters gets an independent backup, and a restore is tested and timed. Cost. A budget, alerts, and a monthly look at cost per useful result.

The account can be explained on one page, and rebuilt from the repository. Deploys stop depending on one person's machine. There's a measured recovery time instead of a guess. The bill has fewer surprises, and often fewer forgotten resources.
The architecture usually stays recognizable. The goal is to make what you have clear, safe, and repeatable, not to rewrite it for the sake of it.

docs.t: Use case: security awareness for a team or family
docs.s: How a typical plain-language security session goes, and what people leave able to do.
k: A typical pattern, not a client story This page describes how this kind of work usually goes. For real projects, see the case studies . Use case: security awareness for a team or family
Someone in the group nearly fell for a fake invoice, a "your account is locked" text, or a call from "the bank." People want to be safer, but most training they've seen was either scary or boring.

A short conversation first about who's in the room, what devices and accounts matter most, and anything that has already happened. One session, about an hour, in plain language, built around real examples: phishing emails and texts, fake support calls, payment fraud, password reuse, and data brokers. Hands-on time. Everyone turns on two-step sign-in for their most important account and checks their recovery details, during the session. A one-page takeaway with what to do when something looks wrong and who to tell. For companies heading into an audit, a separate SOC 2 readiness engagement maps controls, gathers evidence, and fixes the basics before the auditor arrives. The audit opinion itself comes from an independent auditor.
What people leave able to do

Spot the signs of a phishing message and check it a safe way Use a password manager and two-step sign-in on what matters most Recover an account, or know who to call Report something suspicious without feeling foolish
