docs.t: Use case: one workflow, no more retyping
docs.s: How a typical business workflow engagement goes, from the first call to a handover the staff can run.
k: A typical pattern, not a client story This page describes how this kind of work usually goes. For real projects, see the case studies . Use case: one workflow, no more retyping

Requests arrive by web form, email, and phone. Someone copies each one into the scheduling or practice system, then into a spreadsheet to track follow-up. Things get missed or entered twice, and Monday mornings disappear into data entry.

First call, 15 minutes. We find the one workflow that costs the most and check that I'm the right fit. Discovery, a session or two. I watch the real task, time a few examples, and write down what "fixed" looks like and what must not change. Proposal. Options, from a better procedure to configuring what you already pay for to a small integration, each with its ongoing cost and a way out. Build, in small steps. You see a working version early, with made-up data, before anything touches real records. Handover. The person who does the work runs it alone, fixes a deliberate mistake, and keeps a one-page guide. Follow-up, a month later. We compare missed and duplicate requests with the baseline.

Requests land once, in one place, and reach the system of record without retyping. Nothing waits unseen, because a daily summary lists anything unanswered. The tracking spreadsheet is retired, or kept as an export rather than a second copy.
The tools you depend on usually stay. Often the fix is configuring what's already there and adding one small connection.

Intake , discovery record , proposal , release and handover record , and a business associate agreement if health information is involved. The filled-out examples show all of them for a fictional practice.

docs.s: Short answers about using the 1NEON client portal.
k: Short answers about using 1NEON. Signed in? Tap ? at the top right of any page for help with that page.

What is 1NEON? The portal where you and I run your projects together. Each project keeps what you need, the work, the results, and the handover in one place. Watch it . Can I try it first? Yes, three ways, and none needs an account. The guided walkthrough plays a fictional project on the real portal in about a minute, with controls to pause, pick a chapter, or exit; the full story takes about six. The interactive demo is a working copy with made-up clients where you pick who to be and try anything; your changes stay in your browser until you choose Start over . The sample project is one made-up project to read at your own pace, from request to handover. With a minute to spare, start with the walkthrough. Short walkthroughs show a single thing: joining from an invitation , adding a passkey , adding an authenticator app , and texts and text codes . How do I get in? You need an invite. Open the link in your invite email and enter your email address. Sign in with a code sent to your email, or with a passkey. No password needed. Watch it . I didn't get the sign-in code. Check your spam or promotions folder, then wait a minute and choose Send a new code . Codes work for a few minutes, in the browser where you asked for them. Watch it . Is there a tour? Yes. It's offered the first time you sign in. Skip it or ask to be reminded next time, and replay it anytime from ? at the top right or from your profile. Watch it .

What are Needs, Execute, Observe, and Normalize? The four layers every project moves through, N E O N. Needs is what you want and the options to get there. Execute is the work. Observe checks the results against the goals. Normalize makes the change last: handover, training, and care. Watch it . What should I do first on a project? Look at Next step at the top of the project. It says what has to happen now and who it's waiting on, and it changes as soon as that's done: approve an option or send a file and it moves on to the next thing. When nothing is waiting on anyone, it names the stage's goal and offers Move to the next stage. Watch it . What do Not started, On track, At risk, and Off track mean? They're the project's health. A new project is Not started , and it turns On track by itself once it moves past its first stage or any of its work is in progress or done. After that, the team sets it on the project's overview, or with a status update. Items have their own status in their panel: To do, In progress, Blocked, or Done. Watch it . What if we rename, reorder, or hide stages? Projects follow along. Their steps, the board, and Next step use the new names and order. A hidden stage still shows while a project is in it. Decide keeps asking for an approved option, and Closed still ends a project, under any name or position. How do I tell you what I need? Open the project's Needs tab and tap Add request . Finish a sentence with a few taps: what you'd like to do (choose any, or tap + to add your own), what it's for, what happens currently, how often it happens, and when it's due, including a date or a date range. Tap Define another need to add more. Each need becomes its own request, and only the first choice is required. Watch it . Do I have to write a lot? No. Each section says what belongs there, shows an example, and offers suggestions you can add with one tap. Discovery questions take a short answer right where they're asked, and a real example helps most. Watch it . How do I know when something changes? The bell at the top glows softly when something new happens, like a file upload, a decision, or a project moving stage. Tap it to see what changed and who did it, then tap one to open it. Important changes also email you; choose which in your profile under Notifications . Watch it . How do I comment or change an item? Tap the item's title. A panel opens with its status, owner, due date, and details, and a place to comment. Everyone in your organization sees the comments. Options and measures open the same way, with their cost and scores, or unit and target, there too. Watch it . How do I check something off? Tick the box beside it. Every item that can be finished has one, and the counts on each tab and section show how many are done. A choice between options counts as one, done once an option is approved, and a measure counts as done when it reaches its target. Status updates and decisions are records, so they don't count. Files you upload aren't counted either; a File needed is, and it's checked off when you send the file. Watch it . How do I delete something? Use the trash button on the item, or Delete in its panel. Either one asks first. Approved options and decisions can't be deleted, since they're the record of what was agreed; options themselves come from neon1. Files have their own Delete for the person who uploaded them and admins. What does the onion next to a project mean? It shows progress. Needs is the center ring and Normalize is the outside one; each ring fills as that layer's work gets done. What does the board show? Every project as a card, in the stage it's in. Columns run left to right from the first call to care after handover. Drag a card to move it, or use its Move to menu on a phone. A closed project moves back the same way, or use Reopen on its page. Watch it . What does the timeline show? Under Projects , Timeline draws each project from the day it started to its target date, colored by its layer. The dashed line is today, the diamond is the target, the lighter part is time still ahead, and red stripes are time past the target. Each row also says its stage and how many days are left. Watch it . How do I start a project? Choose New project , answer a few short questions, and the project starts with a checklist that fits. You can change everything later. Watch it . What is Coming up on Home? This week and the next two as a strip of days. Each mark is something dated: a task's due date, a milestone, or a project's target. Below it, everything dated in the next six weeks is listed by Overdue, This week, Next week, and Later. Watch it . What is Insights? Charts made from your organization's own data: open and overdue work, how often things finish on time, days to a decision, work finished per week, where projects sit across the four layers, and how healthy they are. Watch it .

How do I approve an option? Open the project's Needs layer, compare the options, and choose Approve this option . You can add conditions, such as "only after 6pm". The approval is recorded with your name, the time, and a copy of the option's terms (title, description, cost, and timeline) exactly as you saw them. Options come from neon1; to ask for a change, comment on the option. Watch it . Who can approve? The person named as the project's decision maker. If nobody is named, an admin of your organization can. Only an admin of your organization can name or change the decision maker, under People on the project's overview, after confirming it's them; editors can change everyone else on the project. Each change is recorded with the old and new decision maker, and neon1 can't be named, since it proposes the options. (In neon1's own organization, where neon1 is the client, it can.) Watch it . Can an approval be changed? Not edited. Once approved, neither the decision nor the option it came from can be edited or removed. To change course, a new option is proposed and approved; the earlier decision stays on record, marked as replaced, so the history stays clear. What do Cost, Quality, and Effort mean? They're neon1's assessment of each option, from 1 to 5, where more filled dots is always better. Cost is the total cost. Quality is how fully it meets the requirements you agreed. Effort is your team's effort to adopt and run it. Each option also lists one-time and recurring charges apart, with a first-year total when it has both; the written price on the option is what you'd agree to. Figures in the demo and the walkthrough are illustrative. Watch it .

How do I send a file? Use Upload next to a file I asked for, or go to Files and upload it there. Pick the project it belongs to. Tap a file's name to open it: PDFs, pictures, and text open in a new tab, and anything else downloads. Watch it . Are files safe? Every file is checked for viruses before anyone can download it, and stays private to your organization. Please don't upload passwords or keys. What can I upload? Any kind of file, up to 100 MB each. Please don't upload passwords, keys, or other secrets, malware, or regulated data such as health or payment card details unless we have a written agreement that covers it.

What can viewers, editors, and admins do? Viewers read and comment. Editors also add and change work. Admins also invite people, change their access, and change settings. neon1's own access is set by neon1, so it shows on People without a way to change it. Watch it . How do I invite someone? Admins go to People and choose Invite people . The person gets an email with a link. People shows whether each invitation email went out; if one didn't, or it got lost, choose Resend . Watch it . Can 1NEON text me? Once texts are switched on, yes. Add your mobile number on your profile, agree to texts, save, then type the code 1NEON texts you. Texts only say that something new is waiting, with a link; they never name your organization, projects, or files. Reply STOP to any text to turn them off. Watch it . Why does it ask me to confirm it's me? Admin actions (inviting people, changing access or settings, and deleting a project or someone else's comment or file) also need a recent confirmation with a passkey, an authenticator app, or a text-message code. That way a stolen email account isn't enough to make changes. On your profile, under Two-step verification, add any of the three, then confirm with it when asked. A second one is a backup if you lose the first. Once confirmed, you won't be asked again for 12 hours in that sign-in. Watch it . Can I use an authenticator app? Yes. On your profile, choose Set up next to Authenticator app, scan the code with Google Authenticator, Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password, Authy, or similar, and type the 6-digit code it shows. Watch it . What's a passkey? A sign-in that uses your face, fingerprint, or device PIN instead of a code. It's faster, and it's phishing-resistant: it only works on the real 1NEON site, so a look-alike page can't use it. Add one on your profile under Two-step verification; next time you sign in, 1NEON offers it first. Watch it .

How do I change my name or the look? Open your profile from the menu. You can change your name, title, theme, menu, and notifications there, then choose Save . The menu button (top left, and Menu at the bottom on phones) opens the full menu; choose Mini to also keep a slim menu of icons on the left. Two-step verification and signing out work right away. Watch it . How do I sign out? Open your profile and choose Sign out . I lost my phone or my authenticator app. You can still sign in with a code sent to your email. The second step is only needed for admin actions, such as inviting people or changing settings. If you set up another method, confirm it's you with that one, then remove the lost one under Two-step verification on your profile and add a new one. If you've lost every method, email hello@neon1.tech from your account's address. The portal has no self-service reset for a lost second step. My email address changed. Your email address is how 1NEON knows you, and it can't be changed on your profile. Ask an admin of your organization to invite your new address and deactivate the old one, or email hello@neon1.tech . Work done under the old address stays in the record under that name. Who do I ask for access? An admin of your organization. Admins invite people and change their access. If you don't know who that is, or neon1's own access needs to change, email hello@neon1.tech .

What does approving an option commit us to? An approval records that your organization agreed to that option as shown: its scope, cost, and timeline, plus any conditions you added. Both sides can rely on that record. It works alongside your signed agreement with neon1, which governs the paid work. Where are invoices and payments? Not in 1NEON. Invoices and payment happen outside the portal, as your signed agreement sets out. Something urgent is wrong. Who do I tell? Email hello@neon1.tech with what happened and when. neon1 is one person working planned hours, with no 24/7 or emergency response, so for something that can't wait, such as a fraud on your bank account or an outage your business can't run without, contact the provider responsible first. Report a security problem in the portal itself to security@neon1.tech . Can we get a copy of our data? Yes. There's no export button, so ask at hello@neon1.tech and I'll send your organization's data in a common format. What happens to our data when the work ends? It's kept as the record of our work together, so either of us can refer back to it, unless your organization asks me to delete it. Your organization can stop using 1NEON at any time and ask for an export first. The privacy policy has the details, including how long backups and audit records last. Who can I contact? Email hello@neon1.tech .

docs.s: Staff spent minutes hunting through Microsoft 365, or interrupted a senior colleague.
k: The firm's knowledge was spread across Microsoft 365: policies, procedure manuals, Word files, PDFs, and client documents. Staff could usually find an answer, but a routine lookup took 2 to 10 minutes, and often meant asking a senior colleague who knew where things lived. Drafts, old versions, and client-restricted files sat right next to the right answer, so a simple chatbot would have been risky. The ask was simple: let staff ask normal questions, return the approved answer with its document, and never make the AI more authoritative than the source.

This was my first project with an AWS partner, Xenoss , who helped with design and now with maintenance. I handled ingestion, embeddings, retrieval, and answer quality. Only documents in approved Microsoft 365 libraries are synced into versioned, encrypted S3, keeping their source, version, and access details. Bedrock Knowledge Bases with Titan embeddings and OpenSearch Serverless run hybrid search, so exact accounting terms and form numbers match as well as differently worded questions. By design, each question is checked against what that person is allowed to see before anything is retrieved, and the assistant is built to answer from the retrieved passages, with citations, or to say it doesn't know. How well it kept to that was measured separately, below. Built with Terraform and deployed through GitHub Actions, with CloudWatch tracking ingestion, retrieval, and answer time separately.

Measure Before After Median lookup, answer and source checked ~4.8 min 13.6 s Slowest 5% of lookups up to 10 min ~24 s Right passage found (recall at 8) 72% 94% Answers fully supported by their source 78% 92% Interruptions of senior staff per week ~18 ~7 Measured on 80 representative questions, including ones the assistant should refuse, and judged by two reviewers. A fast answer from the wrong document counted as a failure. These results describe that test set, not a guarantee. In the evaluation, 92% of answers were fully supported by their source, so the rest were not. Each answer carries its citations so the source can be checked.

Microsoft 365 stays the source of truth, and the search index can be rebuilt from it at any time. The firm owns which documents are approved and who can see them. Next is an MCP server in front of the same retrieval, so assistants and agents can use the firm's knowledge with the same per-person permissions, followed by narrow, reviewable agent actions where they save real time.

docs.t: Intake, out of the shared inbox
docs.s: Intake ran through one inbox, with staff chasing documents and retyping them.
k: A newly opened practice handled intake through a shared Microsoft 365 inbox, and its sister location did the same. Patients replied with forms, insurance cards, referrals, and phone photos. Staff downloaded attachments, renamed them, tracked status in Outlook flags and a spreadsheet, then uploaded each one into a slow EHR. If something was missing, another round of emails began.

I mapped the process with the staff using a questionnaire and conversations, separating the time patients spent waiting from the time staff spent handling documents. Then I built a Terraform-managed serverless portal, with Xenoss helping on design and maintenance. CloudFront, WAF, and a private S3 site serve the portal. API Gateway, Cognito, and Python Lambda run the workflow. Every intake has one clear state in DynamoDB. Documents upload straight to an encrypted S3 vault and stay locked until a malware scan passes. Staff see one queue of what's complete and what's missing. Completed documents are filed into the EHR under the patient's ID and MRN, so they land in the right chart. Email notifications never include patient details, and access, encryption, and audit logging were decided up front.

Measure Before After Median time to a complete intake ~2.6 business days ~3.4 hours Staff time per intake ~24 min ~8 min Finding and opening a document ~2 min 18 s ~12 s Intakes needing a missing-document follow-up ~34% ~10% Four weeks before and four weeks after, with the same definitions. At about 250 intakes a month, the time saved is roughly 67 staff hours a month.
The EHR stays the clinical record. Xenoss and I maintain the portal, watch the intake measures, and tune the workflow as the practice and its sister location grow.

docs.s: The app, database, and files lived on two local servers both offices relied on.
k: An automotive business ran its application, database, and files on two local servers, and both of its locations had to keep working through any move. Their technical lead already patched and supported those servers, so he knew the environment best.

He led the inventory and dependency discovery. I owned the AWS design, sizing, and migration plan. An isolated VPC built with Terraform, EC2 for the application, RDS for the database, and S3 for files that suit object storage. Site-to-Site VPN connects both offices, with separate access paths for the app, the database, and management. Sized from measured CPU, memory, database activity, and storage growth, not by copying the old hardware. Data was seeded ahead of time, and the final cutover kept a fallback ready until both offices signed off.

Check Result Daily business tasks, both offices Passed from each location Records and files after migration Reconciled against the originals Backup and restore Tested with the technical lead Application changes needed None

The technical lead runs the environment, with the architecture, access, backup, restore, and monitoring steps written down. Containers or a bigger platform come later, only if a measured reliability, capacity, or cost problem makes the case.

docs.s: People knew they were exposed online, but not where to start.
k: Teachers, parents, engineers, and executives had the same problem: they knew their accounts, homes, and businesses were exposed, but the security advice they'd seen was too technical or too vague to act on.

I've run sessions at every level, from small groups of parents to cross-team seminars in Manhattan for 30 or more people. Topics include: Securing home and business networks, cameras, and connected devices. Fraud, phishing, data brokers, and what's sold on the dark web. Software and account hygiene, including password managers and two-factor sign-in. The security of physical spaces, not just screens. Each session is built around the devices and accounts that audience uses, with time to change real settings together.

The most useful measure has been what people do afterward: turning on two-factor sign-in during the session, changing default camera and router passwords, and coming back with specific questions about their own setups.

The landscape keeps moving, so the material does too. Ready, Secure, Go, neon1's security readiness guide, tracks what's worth doing for each kind of space, alongside other trusted sources. Companies heading into an audit get SOC 2 and other readiness work.

docs.s: A house with no cameras, and passwords reused everywhere.
k: Not every job is a cloud migration. My parents' house had no camera coverage, and like most families, we reused a handful of passwords across everything.

Planned camera placement around the entrances and blind spots, then installed and configured the system, including recording and alerts. Moved the family onto a password manager, one person at a time, and turned on two-factor sign-in for the accounts that matter most.
The test was simple: could everyone use it without calling me? Recordings and alerts work, and everyone can sign in and find their passwords on their own.
Ongoing advice and troubleshooting when something breaks. Small jobs count too: Wi-Fi that doesn't reach a room, a new laptop, or a grandparent who can't open their email.

docs.s: A grade school wanted real STEM tools on a small budget.
k: A local grade school needed a STEM edtech setup that teachers would use, on a budget with no room for mistakes. I'd wanted to do this kind of work in my own community for some time.

I budgeted the new system, compared the realistic options, and set it up for the classrooms, all as volunteer work. Along the way, I invited teachers and parents to free sessions on staying safe online.
Teachers used it in class, and parents left the sessions with specific steps to take. That showed the same help was worth offering more widely.
That's how neon1 began. Community and nonprofit work is still part of it. Schools and community groups can ask through contact .

k: The neon1 client portal at neon1.tech/1NEON . Each project runs through four layers: Needs, Execute, Observe, and Normalize. Proposals, decisions, files, and results stay together from the first call to handover. Available now, as part of working with neon1. It comes with a client engagement and isn't sold on its own. Who it helps: the people at a client organization who follow a project, send files, and approve options, and the administrators who decide who can see what. For example, I propose two options for a project in the Needs layer. The person named as decision maker compares them and approves one, and 1NEON records their name, the time, and a copy of the option's terms as they saw them.

Access is by invitation only, from neon1 or an administrator of your organization. Invoices and payment happen outside the portal, under your signed agreement. There's no export button. A copy of your organization's data is sent on request. Text messages work only once they're switched on and you've agreed to them on your profile.

See a sample project or try the demo , which runs in your browser with made-up data. To use 1NEON for real, start with a first call . For help inside the portal, see 1NEON help . Code: neon1llc/neon1-1NEON .

docs.s: AWS CLI Plus: account guards and approval checks around the AWS CLI, for people who juggle several AWS profiles.
k: Public · pre-release AWS CLI Plus. Account guards and approval checks around the AWS CLI. It doesn't replace the AWS CLI, which still handles sign-in, credentials, requests, and output. Available now: the code is public and runs from source. It's pre-release, so commands and settings may still change. Who it helps: people who work across several AWS profiles and want to see which account they're in, and confirm before anything risky runs.

Shows where you are. It reports the profile, Region, and the account and role AWS says you're signed in as, and it never prints credential values. Asks before risky commands. Before a command runs, it shows the target profile and Region, the service and operation, and how its policy rules classify it. It doesn't explain every argument: its own previews and plans list option names and leave argument values out, because they can hold sensitive data. Anything that isn't a known read, or that returns credentials or secrets, needs your confirmation. Guards production accounts. A profile can be bound to the account it must resolve to. If it resolves to a different account, the command is refused, and a confirmation can't override that. For example, aws-clip --profile production exec -- ec2 terminate-instances ... shows the target and ec2:terminate-instances , then waits for a yes. If the production profile is bound to an account and resolves to another one, it stops.

AWS output isn't filtered. What the AWS CLI prints, on screen or in logs, can contain sensitive service data. Protect it as you would plain AWS CLI output. Account checks depend on how it's used. Reviewed workflows always check your identity with AWS before the first step. A single command checks the account only when the profile is bound to an account, a policy lists allowed accounts, or you pass --approve-account . Otherwise it runs without that check. Classification goes by operation name , not by what an argument value would do. IAM, service control policies, and your own change process still decide what's allowed.
Read the README for install steps and the full list of safety limits, or browse the code at neon1llc/aws-clip .

docs.s: Cloud automation, bundled: pipelines for infrastructure and applications on any major cloud.
k: Private · pre-release Deploy pipelines for any cloud. A planned bundle of pipelines for infrastructure and applications on AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, or several at once. Not available yet. It's in development and private, with no release date. Who it's for: small technical teams that deploy by hand today, or whose pipelines grew piece by piece. What it's meant to do: set up CI/CD for one repository or many, work with the infrastructure-as-code tools you already use, and add checks, approvals, rollback, monitoring, and alerts where your team will see them. An illustrative example, not a delivered result: a team that deploys a web app by copying files to a server would get a pipeline that runs its checks, waits for an approval, deploys, and can roll back to the last good version.
Nothing here can be installed or tried yet, and the features above may change before it's released.
If you need deploy pipelines now, that work is part of cloud and AI engineering , done as a project with the tools you already use. Get in touch to talk it through.

docs.s: The open-source projects I'd look at first for common small-business needs, what each is for, and what to check before relying on one.
k: A shortlist, not a recommendation These are projects I'd look at first when a need is real. I reviewed their repositories, purpose, and licenses in November 2026. That's discovery, not a production test, a security review, or a promise that any of them suits your business. "Free" software still costs someone's time to host, update, and back up. The technology decisions standard explains how a tool earns its place.

Worth a small trial means a sensible first look when the need exists, often with a hosted version you can pay for instead of running it yourself. Needs an owner means it can be excellent but asks for real technical or domain ownership to run well. In use here means neon1's own public repositories use it today. Projects that usually cost more to run than they save at small-business scale were left off. So were any with an unresolved concern at review time.

k: An example, not legal advice This is an example to show what neon1 LLC agrees to when a project involves protected health information. It follows the structure of the sample provisions published by the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, which says using its sample isn't required for compliance. Your agreement should be reviewed by your own counsel and fitted to your practice, your state, and the actual services. Where a signed agreement differs from this example, the signed agreement governs. This Business Associate Agreement ("Agreement") is made on ("Effective Date") between ("Covered Entity") and neon1 LLC, a New York limited liability company ("Business Associate"), together the "Parties."

Covered Entity and Business Associate have entered, or plan to enter, an agreement for the services described in (the "Services Agreement"). In providing those services, Business Associate may create, receive, maintain, or transmit Protected Health Information on Covered Entity's behalf. The Parties enter this Agreement to meet the requirements of the HIPAA Rules.

Catch-all. Terms used but not defined here, such as Breach, Data Aggregation, Designated Record Set, Disclosure, Health Care Operations, Individual, Minimum Necessary, Notice of Privacy Practices, Required By Law, Secretary, Security Incident, Subcontractor, Unsecured Protected Health Information, and Use, have the meanings given in the HIPAA Rules. HIPAA Rules means the Privacy, Security, Breach Notification, and Enforcement Rules at 45 CFR Part 160 and Part 164. Protected Health Information ("PHI") has the meaning in 45 CFR 160.103, limited to the information Business Associate creates, receives, maintains, or transmits on Covered Entity's behalf.

Business Associate agrees to: Not use or disclose PHI other than as permitted or required by this Agreement or as Required By Law. Use appropriate safeguards, and comply with Subpart C of 45 CFR Part 164 for electronic PHI, to prevent use or disclosure other than as this Agreement provides. Report to Covered Entity any use or disclosure not provided for by this Agreement that it becomes aware of, including Breaches of Unsecured PHI as 45 CFR 164.410 requires, and any Security Incident it becomes aware of, within days of discovery. Unsuccessful attempts that don't result in unauthorized access, such as blocked sign-in attempts and routine network scans, are reported in aggregate on request. Ensure, under 45 CFR 164.502(e)(1)(ii) and 164.308(b)(2), that any Subcontractor that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits PHI on its behalf agrees in writing to the same restrictions, conditions, and requirements. Make PHI in a Designated Record Set available to Covered Entity, or as Covered Entity directs, within days of a request, so Covered Entity can meet 45 CFR 164.524. Make any amendment to PHI in a Designated Record Set that Covered Entity directs or agrees to under 45 CFR 164.526, within days. Keep and provide, within days, the information Covered Entity needs to give an accounting of disclosures under 45 CFR 164.528. To the extent it carries out an obligation of Covered Entity under Subpart E of 45 CFR Part 164, comply with the requirements of Subpart E that apply to Covered Entity in performing that obligation. Make its internal practices, books, and records available to the Secretary for determining compliance with the HIPAA Rules.

Business Associate may use or disclose PHI only as necessary to perform the services in the Services Agreement. Business Associate may use or disclose PHI as Required By Law. Business Associate agrees to make uses, disclosures, and requests for PHI consistent with Covered Entity's minimum necessary policies and procedures. Business Associate may not use or disclose PHI in a way that would violate Subpart E of 45 CFR Part 164 if done by Covered Entity, except as allowed in items 5 and 6. Business Associate may use PHI for its proper management and administration or to carry out its legal responsibilities. Business Associate may disclose PHI for those purposes only if the disclosure is Required By Law, or if Business Associate obtains reasonable written assurances from the recipient that the information will stay confidential, be used or further disclosed only as Required By Law or for the purpose it was disclosed, and that the recipient will notify Business Associate of any known breach of confidentiality. Business Associate will not provide Data Aggregation services, sell PHI, or use PHI for marketing.

Covered Entity will notify Business Associate of: Any limitation in its Notice of Privacy Practices under 45 CFR 164.520, to the extent it may affect Business Associate's use or disclosure of PHI. Any change in, or revocation of, an Individual's permission to use or disclose their PHI, to the extent it may affect Business Associate. Any restriction on use or disclosure Covered Entity has agreed to or must follow under 45 CFR 164.522, to the extent it may affect Business Associate. Covered Entity will not ask Business Associate to use or disclose PHI in any way that wouldn't be allowed under Subpart E of 45 CFR Part 164 if done by Covered Entity.
5. How neon1 handles PHI in practice

These commitments describe how Business Associate meets Section 2 for typical neon1 work. They add to the obligations above and don't narrow them. PHI is accessed only in systems Covered Entity owns or approves, with named accounts, multi-factor sign-in, and the least access the work needs. PHI isn't copied to personal devices, email, chat, or development environments. Development and testing use synthetic or de-identified data. PHI is never entered into an AI service unless Covered Entity approves that service in writing and the service is covered by its own business associate agreement. Access is removed when the services end or are no longer needed, and its removal is confirmed in the handover record. A Subcontractor is used only with Covered Entity's written approval.

Term. This Agreement starts on the Effective Date and ends on or when Covered Entity terminates it for cause, whichever comes first. Termination for cause. If Covered Entity determines that Business Associate has violated a material term, Covered Entity may terminate this Agreement and the Services Agreement if Business Associate doesn't cure the violation within days of written notice. On termination. Business Associate will return to Covered Entity, or with Covered Entity's written agreement destroy, all PHI it still holds in any form, keep no copies, and confirm this in writing. If returning or destroying some PHI isn't feasible, Business Associate will keep it only for the purposes that make return or destruction infeasible, continue to protect it under this Agreement, and not use or disclose it for any other purpose. Survival. Business Associate's obligations under item 3 survive termination.

docs.s: neon1.tech aims for WCAG 2.2 AA. What's in place, what isn't yet, and how to report a barrier.
k: Last updated November 9, 2026. I want everyone to be able to use neon1.tech, the 1NEON portal, and the documents in the Knowledge Center, including people who use a screen reader, a keyboard, magnification, voice control, or reduced motion.
neon1.tech aims to meet the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2 at level AA. This is a target, not a certification, and the site hasn't had a full independent audit.

A "skip to content" link and semantic headings on every page. Navigation and controls built from standard links and buttons, so they work with a keyboard. A pause control for the animated rain. The rain stops when the tab is hidden and becomes a still image when your device asks for reduced motion. The terminal and the white rabbit are optional. Every page and service is reachable without them. Every Knowledge Center PDF has a web page with the same text, and the PDFs are tagged for screen readers.

The white rabbit scene is a 3D animation. It has keyboard controls and a way back that needs no gesture, but it can't be described to a screen reader. Nothing important is only available there. Contrast over the animated rain and the full keyboard path haven't been formally tested against every WCAG criterion yet. Third-party services linked from the site, such as Calendly for booking a call, have their own accessibility. If one doesn't work for you, email or call, and I'll book the call for you.

Every page is validated against the HTML standard on each change, and keyboard and reduced-motion behavior is checked by hand during development. A full review with automated accessibility tools and a screen reader is planned, and this statement will be updated with what it finds.

If something on neon1.tech or in a neon1 document doesn't work for you, please tell me at hello@neon1.tech or call (424) 326-3661 . Say which page and what happened, if you can. I'll reply within a few days, and I'll get you the information in a way that works for you while I fix it.

k: Last updated November 10, 2026. This update corrects how the policy describes things the portal already does: where the authenticator app key is kept, which emails and texts you can get (there is no daily summary), and how Neo handles questions. It adds no new use of your information. neon1 LLC ("neon1", "I", "me") runs the website neon1.tech and the 1NEON client portal at neon1.tech/1NEON. This policy explains what information I collect, why, and what you can do about it.

The website has no analytics, ads, or trackers, and sets no cookies. The 1NEON portal stores only what's needed to run your projects with me, and it uses only the cookies that keep you signed in. I never sell or rent your information, and I never use it for advertising.

On the website. No accounts, analytics, or tracking. Like any website, the servers that deliver it (Amazon CloudFront) handle your IP address and browser details to send you the pages, and AWS may keep them briefly for security and operations. Your browser saves the rain display settings you pick, on your device only. If you use Neo, the assistant on the website and in the portal, your questions are answered by a model (Qwen3 Next 80B) on Amazon Bedrock, in AWS's US East (N. Virginia) region, which writes an answer from neon1's public pages. Neo's service doesn't log or store the text of your questions or its answers; its logs hold only details such as timing, length, and errors. Bedrock's own logging of questions and answers is turned off in my AWS account. To notice the same question sent over and over, Neo keeps a one-way fingerprint of it for ten minutes, and the question limits count visitors by a one-way code, not by IP address. How AWS itself handles requests is set out in Amazon's Bedrock documentation . Please don't type anything sensitive into Neo. If you email me or book a call through Calendly, I receive what you send, such as your name, email address, and message. Calendly handles bookings under its own privacy policy. In the 1NEON portal , which is available only to people invited by me or by an administrator of their organization: Account details: your email address, and optionally your name, job title, phone number, and profile photo. Sign-in data: your sign-in methods (email codes, passkeys, Google sign-in, an authenticator app, or a password) and security events, such as sign-in times, the IP address and browser used, and when a sign-in method was added or removed. Passwords, passkeys, and email codes are handled by Amazon Cognito, and I never see your password. Authenticator app key: if you set up an authenticator app, the portal itself creates the app's secret key and keeps it so it can check your 6-digit codes. It's stored in the portal's database, encrypted at rest, read only by the portal's server to check a code, shown to you once during setup and never again, and deleted when you remove the app. An unfinished setup is discarded after 10 minutes. Project content: what you and your colleagues add to the portal, such as requirements, decisions, tasks, metrics, comments, and files. Activity records: who changed what and when, kept as an audit trail so both sides have a reliable history of the work. Please don't put passwords, keys, or other secrets in the portal. The portal is not designed for health, payment, or other regulated personal data, and I won't take on work involving such data until the right agreement (for example, a business associate agreement) is in place.

To provide the portal: signing you in, showing your organization's projects, and sending the emails you need (invitations, sign-in codes, and notices about the kinds of changes you choose, each of which you can turn off in your profile). To keep the portal secure: detecting misuse, investigating incidents, and keeping an audit trail. To communicate with you about the work we're doing together. I don't use your information for marketing, and I don't use automated decision-making that affects you. Text messages. If you add a mobile number and agree to texts in your profile, 1NEON first texts a 6-digit code to that number to confirm it's yours (only a one-way code of it is stored, and it expires in 10 minutes). After that, 1NEON texts you about the kinds of changes you choose, such as file uploads or a project moving stage. Each text says only that something new is waiting, with a link to sign in; it doesn't name your organization, project, or files. Changing your number turns texts off until the new number is confirmed. Message frequency varies with your projects, up to 10 notices a day. Message and data rates may apply. Reply STOP to any text to opt out, or HELP for help, and you can turn texts off in your profile at any time. A STOP reply is recorded on your profile, and turning texts back on needs a new code. Your number and your agreement are used only to send these notices. I never sell or share mobile numbers or text consent with third parties or affiliates for their marketing.

I use a small number of service providers, each only for the purpose listed: Provider Purpose Amazon Web Services (United States) Hosting, storage, sign-in, email and text message delivery, and answers from Neo, the site's assistant Google (Google sign-in, Google Workspace) Optional sign-in with Google; my business email Calendly Booking calls from the website I disclose information only to these providers, when the law requires it, or to protect the rights and safety of people using neon1's services.
Where it's stored and how long

Portal data is stored in the United States on AWS, encrypted in transit and at rest. Each organization's data is kept separate from every other organization's. Account and project data: kept as the record of our work together, including after an engagement ends, so either of us can refer back to it. Your organization can ask me to delete it at any time, and I will, unless the law requires me to keep something. Deleted items: projects moved to the trash are hidden from everyone but kept, and erased if your organization asks. Deleted files are removed right away. Database backups roll off after 35 days, and earlier copies of deleted or replaced files after 90 days. Audit records: kept for up to 3 years. Messages on their way: emails and texts wait in a short queue until they're sent. A record that one was delivered, or that one failed after its retries, is kept for 30 days so I can find and fix delivery problems, then removed.

You can view and update your profile at any time in the portal. You can also ask me to: give you a copy of your information, or your organization's data, in a common format; correct or delete your information; or stop sending you non-essential emails or texts. Your organization's administrator controls who can access its workspace. If a request concerns your organization's project content, I may need to involve that administrator. I'll respond within 30 days. Depending on where you live, you may have additional rights under laws such as the GDPR or state privacy laws, and you can complain to your local data protection authority.
The website sets no cookies. The portal uses only strictly necessary cookies. See the cookie and storage notice for those cookies and what each site saves in your browser.
neon1's services are for adults and businesses. I don't knowingly collect information from children under 13.

k: Last updated November 9, 2026. If you think you've found a security problem in neon1.tech, the 1NEON portal, Neo, or any neon1llc repository , thank you. Please tell me privately so it can be fixed before anyone else finds it.

Email security@neon1.tech . If that bounces, use hello@neon1.tech . Please don't open a public issue. Helpful details include: What you found and where (the URL, repository, or file) Steps to reproduce it What someone could do with it How you'd like to be credited, if at all

I'll acknowledge your report within a few days. I'll keep you updated while I investigate and fix it. Once it's fixed, I'll credit you publicly if you want. There's no bug bounty. neon1 is a one-person company, and I can't offer payment.

Access, change, or delete other people's data, including 1NEON workspaces that aren't yours. Run automated scans that put real load on the site, Neo, or the portal. Try phishing, social engineering, or physical attacks. Share the problem publicly before it's fixed.
If you act in good faith and follow this policy, I won't pursue legal action over your research, and I'll work with you to understand and fix the problem.

In scope: neon1.tech and its subpaths, including the 1NEON portal and Neo's chat, and the public neon1llc repositories. Out of scope: third-party services neon1 uses, such as Amazon Web Services, GitHub, Google, and Calendly. Please report those to their owners.
